item.title: The Health Benefits of Humor and Laughter for Seniors
item.description:
Humor

The Health Benefits of Humor and Laughter for Seniors

Humor heals—even when you don't laugh.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Humor supports physical, emotional, cognitive, and social well-being as we age.
  • Laughter, wit, mirth, and relational fusion offer distinct benefits beyond laughter alone.
  • Humor can shift perspective, ease distress, strengthen relationships, and build resilience.
Source: steve sultanoff

Most people think humor and laughter are the same. They are not. Laughter is physical and physiological. Humor can also change how we think, feel, and connect with others—even when no laughter occurs.

As we grow older, we face health challenges, loss, changing roles, reduced mobility, and/or increased isolation. One of the most accessible tools for enhancing well-being is humor.

Humor benefits us through four interconnected domains:

  1. Laughter—physical and physiological; affects the body
  2. Wit—cognitive; refreshes the mind
  3. Mirth—emotional; lifts the heart
  4. Relational fusion—social and interpersonal; strengthens relationships

1. Laughter: The Physical and Physiological Benefits

Laughter is a physical experience that can produce muscle relaxation and reduce tension. Laughter has been associated with beneficial changes in stress physiology, pain tolerance, cardiovascular functioning, respiration, and immune functioning.

For seniors, one finding is particularly intriguing: Humor and laughter appear to increase tolerance for pain, and increased pain tolerance is welcome as our bodies accumulate those annoying reminders that we aren't 25 anymore.

2. Wit: The Cognitive Benefits

Wit is the cognitive dimension of humor—the shift that occurs when we suddenly see something differently. Humor can interrupt rigid thinking patterns and help us view a situation from another angle.

That becomes particularly valuable as seniors encounter the losses, frustrations, limitations, and unexpected changes that accompany aging. Humor doesn't make difficult circumstances disappear, but it can change the lens through which we view them.

Developing a comic vision—the ability to notice and appreciate the humorous side of everyday life—can help us manage life's inevitable irritations. Humor doesn't make the big stuff small, but it can help us recognize when we're turning the small stuff into big stuff.

3. Mirth: The Emotional Benefits

Humor also influences how we feel by activating mirth—the uplifting emotional response to a humorous experience. Mirth includes amusement, delight, joy, playfulness, or simply a feeling of lightness. Mirth can interrupt distressing emotions and give us an emotional breather.

As we age, mirth can help us cope with loss, changes in abilities, retirement, altered family roles, health concerns, or uncertainty about the future. Humor doesn't erase grief, anxiety, anger, or sadness. Instead, it gives us access to another emotional experience alongside them.

4. Relational Fusion: The Social Benefits

I coined the term relational fusion to describe the emotional bond created when people share humor. It acts as both a social glue and an interpersonal lubricant.

For older adults, this can be particularly important because retirement, illness, reduced mobility, or loss can lead to social isolation.

I experienced a brief interaction of relational fusion at Costco. I went to the gift-card window and told the employee, "I'm here to pick up my special-order cake."

She looked momentarily confused, then smiled when she recognized the absurdity.

"I'll settle for two gift cards," I said.

She handed me the cards and replied, "Thank you. I needed a stress break."

For a few seconds, two strangers connected. That was relational fusion—and neither of us needed to fall over laughing for it to happen.

Humor Is More Than Laughter

Together, laughter, wit, mirth, and relational fusion illustrate why humor is much more than laughter. These domains interact: a humorous thought may generate mirth; mirth may produce laughter; and shared laughter may create relational fusion.

Four Daily Humor Habits

  1. Collect one funny every day. Become a humor hunter. Keep a humor log. Looking for one "funny" each day—a clever sign, unexpected comment, cartoon, or humorous moment trains you to notice humor rather than waiting for it to find you. At the end of the day, ask yourself, “What tickled me today?”
  2. Revisit a favorite humor memory. You have a treasure trove of what I call humor happenings—humorous moments from your life. Recall the people, sights, sounds, and circumstances surrounding those humorous moments.
  3. Share humor with someone. Share a humorous story, cartoon, playful observation, joke, or funny memory. Ask friends and family to recall shared mirthful memories. Shared humor becomes part of the emotional history of a relationship.
  4. Keep a playful prop nearby. Keep something within easy reach that invites play—a clown nose, bubbles, silly pen, funny button, or anything else that tickles your fancy. Small playful cues remind us that life doesn't always have to be taken quite so seriously.

Can You Develop a Better Sense of Humor?

You do not need to tell jokes or become the funniest person in the room. Instead, learn to notice, appreciate, and participate in the humor already around you. The more frequently you look for humor, the more likely you are to find it. Eventually, your comic vision can become automatic.

The greatest benefit of humor may come not from occasional comedy but from integrating humor into everyday life—finding it in conversations, signs, mistakes, memories, unexpected situations, and the absurdities that surround us. Eventually, humor can become less something we do and more part of how we experience life.

From the Psychologist's Couch

During many decades working as a psychologist with older adults, I've repeatedly seen humor become an unexpected source of resilience, connection, and healing.

One older client who was extremely serious and emotionally flat discovered email. Yes, this was a long time ago.

Unexpectedly, he began emailing me jokes, anecdotes, and cartoons. Eventually, sharing humor electronically evolved into sharing humor during our sessions. He became increasingly animated and energized, opening a new aspect to our therapeutic work.

Aging may give us even more opportunities to appreciate life's absurdities, cherish shared memories, and enjoy playful moments with the people who matter to us.

Humor won't eliminate life's challenges. But it can change how we experience them.

Every smile, moment of mirth, fresh perspective, and shared laugh is a small investment in healthier thinking, stronger relationships, greater resilience, and a richer quality of life.

item.title: 3 Ways AI May Be Hurting Your Executive Function
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

3 Ways AI May Be Hurting Your Executive Function

Harness AI’s help without accidentally impairing your abilities.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • AI can provide tools like organizing and task breakdowns, which can support executive function tasks.
  • Overuse of AI can atrophy your skill set.
  • Misusing AI may diminish your self-trust and pride in your work.

I’m collaborating with a well-respected colleague in the ADHD world when she pauses, for at least the fifth time, to consult ChatGPT. She wants to know when to schedule an online parent event for the best attendance. Chat doesn’t offer just one solution; instead, it offers several options that include morning, afternoon, and evening times, and I watch her face try to reconcile that even after getting an “answer,” she still doesn’t feel clear. She rephrases the query and asks again, getting a new, longer list of options. In the process, ChatGPT praises her for continuing to ask such great questions.

She finally asks me what I think. I share my experiences with attendance for online events, and offer that considering both the audience needs and realities usually gives a few ideas for timeframes. We could even ask a few of the people we’re trying to attract to the event, I suggest. Our process takes a few minutes and texts to three parents we know. We come away with an awareness of when not to schedule events for parents, an understanding of how long events can reasonably be, and even a strategy for reminding our busy guests. The template we’ve built by slogging through the cognitive process will serve us in the future. If ChatGPT had assumed the cognitive load, we’d depend on it again in a few months to help us solve the very same schedule problem, and we would have missed the awareness that we need to also adjust event reminders for our audience.

Robots are cute, but they can't be your brain replacement.
Source: Alex Knight/Pexels

Students and Young Adults Outsourcing Thinking to AI

I’m seeing this pattern emerge with students and young adults in my executive function coaching. The realities of exhaustion, stress, and busy schedules entice them to consult AI to think for them: write an email, draft a reply for a discussion board, or even complete an entire assignment. The short-term win in time saved feels immediate and rewarding, and I truly understand the temptation. However, three big concerns are emerging around using AI for executive function tasks:

First, executive function represents a skill set that we can almost think of like mental muscles; stop using them, and they atrophy. In reflective moments, my clients will share regret that they’ve forgotten how to do tasks like writing an email or even making a meal plan because they’ve outsourced the executive function workout to AI. Feeling less confident after not using these executive function skills, they end up turning back to AI, again reducing their chances of growing their mental muscles.

A second concern relates to self-concept and pride: over time, my clients who use AI to complete executive function tasks begin to doubt they could do them on their own. When I praise them for work that I didn’t know was done mostly by AI, they tend to shrink a little, sometimes admitting that Claude earned that positive praise, not them. I feel like I’m watching their self-efficacy diminish, and we explore ways to put them back in the leading position so AI provides tools, not a mental takeover.

article continues after advertisement

My third, and maybe most painful, observation of AI's impact on executive function and my clients is that it tends to destroy the beauty that comes from their amazing, divergent-thinking brains. My clients are people who can think in non-linear ways, who can problem-solve based on a detail others may have dismissed, who can use bottom-up thinking to create a brand-new perspective, humor, or art. Their brains can feel messy, yes, but from that mess comes some of the world’s best ideas. When AI gets to take over the thinking or executive function processes, it provides a mashup of ideas scoured from the internet and its learned language models—models that are based on largely neurotypical authors and studies. Diluting these important perspectives and voices robs all of us of the richness that results from the representation of all brains.

Over-reliance on AI could atrophy your executive function skills.
Source: cottonbro studios/Pexels

How to Build Executive Function Without Losing Your Voice

AI can provide great tools, models, and templates to help us get unstuck, see new ways to approach a problem, or help provide scaffolding as we build new skills. However, an over-reliance on AI tools may be doing more harm to our executive function skills than we realize. It’s important for each of us to reflect on how and when AI is helping us and how and when it’s simply doing our mental work for us. I promise the growth that comes from sticking with yourself in the messy moments is always worth it. I know it is, ChatGPT said so, too. Just kidding.

item.title: Hypnosis May Mitigate the Nocebo Response
item.description:
Placebo

Hypnosis May Mitigate the Nocebo Response

The neurobiology of nocebo and hypnosis affect similar areas of the brain.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • The nocebo effect can occur when patients are informed of potential side-effects during a consent process.
  • Nocebo effects have been linked to the activation of brain stress pathways.
  • Self-hypnosis calming techniques may be an effective way of mitigating nocebo responses.
Source: Parichat Photo/Shutterstock

Negative expectations can cause or increase symptoms and side-effects beyond the physiological effects of a treatment. These responses are referred to as nocebo effects.

The nocebo effect can occur because of (Häuser, et al., 2012):

  • Being informed of potential side-effects during a consent process. For instance, this can occur upon enrollment in a research study, or when patients are being told about risks of a medical procedure.
  • Negative past experiences with treatments or environmental exposures. For instance, patients who have developed side-effects after taking previous medications, are more likely to develop side-effects from new medications (Planès, 2016). Patients with asthma who have developed shortness of breath after exposure to an allergen are more likely to develop shortness of breath when they think they have been exposed to this allergen, even in the absence of such exposure (Luparello, 1968).
  • Negative clinical interactions with a clinician or medical facility that lead to mistrust. An unfavorable treatment environment may also influence patients' expectations and trust, potentially contributing to nocebo responses. (Kothari, 2026).

Interestingly, the type of side-effects that patients develop because of a nocebo effect depends on (1) the possible side-effects from a drug or procedure that they have learned about through a consent process (Amanzio, et al., 2009); (2) whether they have experienced or observed people who have developed certain side-effects following a treatment or exposure (Vögtle, et al., 2013); or (3) when they have heard in the media of particular side-effects as being associated with a particular treatment (Asan, et al., 2024).

The Neurobiology of Nocebo

Nocebo effects have been linked to the activation of brain stress pathways involving the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, increased cortisol release, and activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and periaqueductal gray (PAG) (Raghuraman & Colloca, 2025).

For instance, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have shown that expectations of increased pain are associated with greater brain activity in regions involved in pain processing and emotional regulation, including the PFC, ACC, and PAG. This can lead patients to have an increased subjective experience of pain.

Furthermore, negative expectations leading to increased pain from nocebo have been associated with two biochemical pathways strongly linked to stress reactions: cholecystokinin secretion and HPA axis activity.

How can the Nocebo Effect Be Minimized?

Given that nocebo response can decrease the effectiveness of therapy, and can even preclude the use of therapy in some patients, several methods have been proposed to reduce the nocebo response that can arise because of the informed consent process (Häuser, et al., 2012):

article continues after advertisement
  • The perceived tolerability of a new treatment might be improved by decreased focus regarding potential side-effects in a minority of patients and instead emphasizing that the great majority of patients have tolerated the treatment well.
  • Before providing a drug, patients can be asked if they agree not to receive information about mild side-effects. In this setting, patients must nonetheless be told about potential severe side-effects.
  • Increased patient education provided by a pharmacist has been shown to reduce the rate of side-effects in patients with chronic pain.

A Neurobiological Rationale for Hypnosis Interactions with Nocebo

Beyond modifications to the informed consent process, I hypothesize that the use of hypnosis may offer a more direct neurobiological intervention which addresses the underlying mechanisms of the nocebo response.

Based on our understanding of the neurobiology of hypnosis, this method could potentially intervene at many levels of the nocebo response:

  • The HPA axis is the body's primary stress response system and cortisol is the primary glucocorticoid released because of HPA axis activation. Cortisol is both a marker of stress and a cause of on-going stress reactions. Recent research suggests that hypnosis-based safety suggestions can influence physiological stress responses, including reducing the cortisol response (Schmidt et al., 2026)
  • The ACC plays a central role in pain processing and the integration of emotional and cognitive responses to threat (Rainville, 1997), such as occurs in the nocebo response. Through neuroimaging studies, hypnosis has been shown to alter ACC activation during pain processing, thereby reducing the unpleasantness of pain (Faymonville et al., 2000).
  • Memories of negative experiences can contribute to subsequent nocebo responses (Eichenbaum & Cohen, 2014). Hypnotic reframing can reduce the emotional intensity associated with the recall of distressing memories (Bryant & Fearns, 2007). In addition, hypnotic suggestions may help patients develop new interpretations and expectations that compete with previously learned negative associations (Oakley & Halligan, 2013).
  • The PAG is a midbrain structure that is an important pathway through which endogenous opioids suppress pain signals traveling up from the body. The nocebo effect appears to suppress PAG-mediated pain inhibition which leads to pain signals to be amplified rather than suppressed (Crawford et al., 2021). Hypnosis-facilitated positive expectation and relaxation may enhance PAG-mediated inhibition, potentially counteracting nocebo-driven pain facilitation. (Faymonville, et al., 2000).
article continues after advertisement

Case Example

The patient through whom I first learned about hypnosis was a 17-year-old named Paul who was very allergic to milk products. He showed me that when he thought about eating a cheeseburger, he developed severe breathing problems.

I taught Paul how to use hypnosis to calm himself. Several months later, he had inadvertently eaten a milk product and struggled to breathe despite use of intramuscular epinephrine. His ER physicians decided that he was struggling so much that he would require placement of a tube into his throat so that they could assist him with use of a mechanical ventilator (as had occurred on two previous occasions in his life).

At that time, Paul decided to use hypnosis to calm himself. This helped his breathing stabilize and he did not require a breathing tube.

In this case, hypnosis appeared to help reduce Paul's distress and stabilize his breathing sufficiently to avoid intubation. Given his history of severe reactions, it is likely that a nocebo effect contributed to his respiratory distress in addition to the underlying allergic reaction, and that hypnosis helped ease this distress.

However, this case cannot establish how much of his improvement was attributable to hypnosis, and hypnosis should not be considered a substitute for epinephrine or emergency treatment of anaphylaxis.

Takeaway

A meta-analysis of 10 studies has demonstrated that patients who are highly responsive to suggestions are more apt to develop a nocebo response (Stein, et al., 2025). These patients’ high suggestibility could mean that they are both more vulnerable to nocebo and more responsive to hypnotic countersuggestion.

The neurobiology of nocebo responses suggests a potential role for hypnosis in their reduction. Negative expectations can activate stress and pain-facilitation systems, whereas hypnotic suggestions can positively influence expectations, emotional reactions, autonomic stress responses, and pain processing.

Thus, I hypothesize that teaching self-hypnosis calming techniques may be an effective way of mitigating nocebo responses, especially in patients who are highly suggestible. This hypothesis should be tested in future research studies.

item.title: Understanding the Role of Anger in Physical Punishment
item.description:
Anger

Understanding the Role of Anger in Physical Punishment

Reducing physical punishment starts with understanding the anger that fuels it.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Anger is a feeling that drives behavior. It signals to ourselves and others that something is wrong.
  • Distress can quickly pile up to anger, past what we can regulate. Even excitement can trigger it.
  • Anger is contagious, so physical punishment often angers the child, the parent, and onlookers alike
  • Try curiosity: What set off the anger, why now? Distract youngsters with games or songs.

Anger—we have all felt it, heard it, and seen it in ourselves and others. In this discussion, I want to look at the role anger has in physical punishment. I suggest that by better understanding anger, we have a better chance of understanding and decreasing physical punishment. So, first, we will explore what anger is from a variety of perspectives, and then focus on its role in physical punishment.

What Is Anger?

Anger seems so often to be misunderstood. Anger is a feeling. Feelings cause behaviors.

Feelings (or “affects”) are reactions to internal and external stimuli, contributing to our motivations, behaviors, communication, and emotional development.

According to the late psychologist Silvan Tomkins, anger is one of our nine basic feelings. The others are interest and enjoyment (positive feelings); surprise (resetting); and distress, fear, shame, disgust (reaction to unpleasant tastes), and dissmell (reaction to unpleasant odors) (negative feelings) (Tomkins, 1991, Holinger, 2025).

Anger, like all feelings, is a signal—to oneself and to others. Anger could be termed an SOS signal, a call for help: “Something is wrong here!” As Tomkins notes, “All the negative affects trouble human beings deeply… Anger is problematic above all” (1991, p.111).

And as Aristotle noted in The Nicomachean Ethics in 340 BC, “Anyone can get angry—that is easy… but to do this to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive, and in the right way, that is not for everyone, nor is it easy.”

Anger is linked to the affect of distress. Everyone has a stimulus threshold that can trigger distress and then anger. So anger is excessive distress—“too muchness.”

With infants and young children, any excessive sustained increase in the level of stimulation, such as a bright light, loud noise, hunger, fatigue, or illness, may activate distress: annoyance, irritability, arched eyebrows, corners of the mouth turned down, tears and crying, and so on. If the stimulation persists and heightens, anger is triggered: frowning eyebrows, narrowed eyes, red face, the roar of rage.

With older children and adults, the stimuli may be quite varied: stress involving school pressures, parental expectations, peers; work, children, spouse; physical pain; conscious and unconscious fantasies; and so on. Distress increases, and annoyance, irritability, and snippiness can morph into anger.

Anger might be termed a quantitative affect: There is “too muchness,” too much stress and stimulation. The term stressed out is appropriate. Stress may increase incrementally, the straw that breaks the camel’s back. Things may be going along reasonably well, but then one event after another begins to push the envelope toward anger. Any one, or two, or three of these issues might be easily handled, but too many of them piled up exceed the individual’s tension-regulatory capacity and lead to anger. These processes have important implications for the regulation of feelings and behaviors.

It is interesting to note that any affect, positive or negative, if excessive enough, can produce anger. For example, too much excitement can lead to anger; if a decrease in stimulation (enjoyment) is too much, this can lead to boredom, irritability, and anger; a too-intense startle episode can result in fear and anger. Anger is also a final common pathway for all the negative affects. Excessive distress, fear, shame, disgust, and dissmell can all ultimately trigger an anger response. This is important clinically and in daily life, especially with respect to understanding anger that may have roots in excessive fear or shame.

Anger is also what might be termed a contagious affect—anger in one person can readily elicit anger in another. How and why? How—probably because someone else’s anger adds to another person's level of distress. Think of a car honking behind you, or road rage. This increase in stimulation can feel like an attack, an assault, or a warning about your own behavior.

Why is anger contagious? Probably, from an evolutionary perspective, because anger in another person creates enough stimulation to elicit a startle response, or distress, or anger, in order to respond to a potential threat.

Although anger may be the basic affect, there are many words used to describe different aspects of anger. This can sometimes enhance or confuse the understanding of anger in clinical as well as everyday circumstances. Consider, for example, annoyance, irritability, hostility, rage, viciousness, aggression, and destruction.

Whose Anger Is Involved?

Who is getting angry during episodes of physical punishment, that is, spanking, hitting, pinching, and so on? Nearly everyone! Or in other words, whose feelings of distress are increasing to anger in response to these behaviors?

Quite a few people may be involved. First of all, the child him or herself. Second, whoever is doing the hitting—parents, caregivers, and so on. Observers may feel distress and get angry.

Sometimes the distress and anger are subtle. In addition, the rage directed at the child may be accompanied by a sense of enjoyment, for a variety of reasons.

The major issues here involve the number of people who can become involved and be angry, with potentially increasing distress and actions.

Where Does This Anger Come From?

From whom and what does this anger originate? What kind of distress—internal or external, past or present—triggers the anger?

For example, the anger can come:

  • From the child becoming increasingly distressed about having to do or stop something.
  • From the parents, due to the child’s behavior, or perhaps because of what was done to them by their own parents and/or caregivers.
  • From anyone’s own internal world; rage at the child for disobeying; fear that the child might get hurt, e.g., running into the street.

The possibilities are endless.

Stopping Physical Punishment

  1. The first order of business is understanding the affect of anger. Feelings (affects) cause behaviors. Anger begins with the feeling of distress, and as distress increases, the classic signs of anger emerge, and then rage. Anger is too muchness, too much stimulation, too much disorganization.
  2. Second, the feeling of interest (curiosity) is extremely useful. What set off the anger?
    Why now? Does it happen frequently? Can the issues be talked about?
  3. Third, with the children, discussion can be: What can distract the youngster from this increasing disorganization? A song, a game, a funny noise, a lovey or teddy bear type of thing?

Wrapping Up

Humans have three basic information processing systems: feelings, cognition, and language. These three information processing systems can all be useful in understanding and dealing with anger (Holinger, 2025; Tomkins, 1991).

Feelings contribute to our various behaviors and motivations. Cognition includes thinking, self-reflection, learning, and more. Language involves putting words and symbols to feelings.

Also, the process of introspection is useful and crucial in understanding and dealing with physical punishment. Being able to look inside ourselves—using feelings, cognition, and language—can make a world of difference in dealing with anger and curing physical punishment. In addition, being empathic with others in the midst of these events can be extraordinarily helpful. This is called vicarious introspection (Kohut, 1959).

item.title: When Your Adult Child Doesn't Live Up to Your Hopes
item.description:
Family Dynamics

When Your Adult Child Doesn't Live Up to Your Hopes

How parents can handle the disappointment of unmet expectations.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Parents often feel angry, ashamed, and bereaved when adult children don't fulfill their dreams.
  • When we are emotionally distraught, we tend to put ourselves at physical and emotional risk.
  • Untangling the family dynamics is key to the healing process.
Source: Ines Pavao / Pexels

"My daughter and I were so close. I never imagined she would get married, have kids, and cut me off. She doesn't answer my phone calls, texts, or emails and practically forbids my grandchildren from speaking with me. It's hurtful beyond words. Her husband refuses to talk to us and clearly considers any involvement we try to have with their family an intrusion. I can handle him not liking us, but what happened to my daughter? Doesn't she remember the close relationship we had? I don't even know who she is anymore." –Cynthia, 68

"Our son was a sweet kid, a good student, and became a successful graphic artist. He married a lovely woman, and they have an adorable young son. He seemed happy. One minute everything seemed to be going smoothly, and the next minute, he tells us he wants out of his marriage. He's now divorced, strapped for money, and acts like a different person. We try to be emotionally supportive, but he's irritable, impatient, and angry with us all the time. He doesn't say why. It's almost as if he is blaming us for choosing the wrong partner and things not going well in his life. What are we supposed to do when our child is all grown up but acts like a defiant teen?" –Noah, 70

Parenting Adult Children

Throughout my years of practicing psychiatry, I've seen endless variations of parents who are disappointed, angry, embarrassed, ashamed, and devastated when their adult child doesn't meet their expectations. I've had patients who are upset because their adult children are too religious, not religious enough, too emotionally needy, too emotionally rejecting, failures in their careers, and so successful that they don't appreciate all their parents did to help them get to where they are. They may be upset that their adult child never visits them or visits them too much. Some feel their children are too demanding of financial support, while others are accused of spoiling their grandchildren by giving them too many gifts.

At a time in their lives when they expected they would be finished dealing with parental challenges, they find themselves confused and in despair that things didn't work out with their kids the way they wanted. Their frustration and sadness are palpable.

Sorting Through the Chaos

There is almost a sense of mourning that parents may experience when their adult children don't fulfill their expectations. Whether they find fault with their children's career path, lifestyle choices, attitudes, or behaviors, they are grieving a future they imagined but has not been realized. These are tumultuous feelings that need to be teased apart to find a healthy approach with which to move forward.

article continues after advertisement
  • The first step: Try to get to the root of the problem. If there is an estrangement, I ask if my patient knows what they may have done to spark that. Have they tried to communicate with their adult child to clarify what is causing the alienation? Is there something that can be "fixed"? Is there an apology that can rectify the situation? Can reaffirming one's love smooth over "ruffled feathers"?
  • The second step: Establish healthy boundaries. As parents of adult children, we can offer empathy and guidance and maybe even help in a practical way by providing babysitting or temporary financial or housing assistance. But we can't rescue them. Our adult children need to be empowered to problem-solve on their own and move forward in their lives. Sometimes all we can do is model for them a healthy attitude. That means we can't fall apart because they are going through a hard time. We don't need to feel guilty and assume we did something wrong because our expectations weren't fulfilled. While we do everything we can to influence our children when they are young, they each need to pursue their individual path. We love our children, but we can't control them. Accepting their separate identity and developing a healthy sense of detachment can be key components of therapy.
  • The third step: Ensure your own well-being. Parents who are suffering because their adult children are causing them heartache must protect themselves from making themselves sick. When we are emotionally distraught, we tend not to take care of ourselves. We put ourselves at physical and emotional risk. At times, I see parents who feel so betrayed or disappointed by their adult children that they become practically paralyzed. They feel hopeless and helpless, and have lost their ability to enjoy life. In these situations, psychiatric medication may be appropriate to ensure their mood (sadness, irritability), cognitive (lack of focus, poor decision-making), and somatic (sleeping, eating, and other physical problems) symptoms don't intensify. For parents who become overwhelmed by regrets regarding how they parented, we work through those memories and feelings—trying to understand what happened in the past, why it happened, and how one can handle the present situation in the healthiest and most productive way possible.
  • The fourth step: Keep the rest of your family intact. Problems with adult children often spark other rifts. The tension of dealing with family troubles can create a vicious cycle in which unhappiness about one problem (an adult child who is a disappointment) triggers couple conflict, blame, tension with other adult children, or even resentment toward other relatives who take sides and think they are helping by intervening. If you find tensions escalating throughout the family, consult a marital or family therapist. Do everything possible to contain this issue and not let it take over your life.
  • The fifth step: Identify areas of life that provide satisfaction and joy. With time, many adult child/parent conflicts resolve. I certainly encourage my patients to do all they can to rectify hurt feelings and come to a mutual understanding with family members. However, whether that occurs or not, it is vital to recognize that there are some things in life we do not control. Ultimately, the one thing in life we do control is our attitude. Determine what activities bring you joy. Whether it is reading mysteries, dancing Zumba, practicing yoga, playing chess or Mah Jongg, eating out at restaurants, traveling, going to the movies...whatever it might be, do it! Fill your time with activities that nourish your heart and mind. Parenting is a journey. We all do the best we can. Shape your life to the best it can be.

item.title: The Myth of Catharsis and Bottling It Up
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

The Myth of Catharsis and Bottling It Up

Only when emotion is elicited in safety can we hope for a therapeutic outcome.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Only when emotion is elicited in safety can we hope for a therapeutic outcome.
  • A popular misconception persists that emotional expression is of itself therapeutic.
  • The insights from trauma work should be applied to the whole field of psychotherapy.
Source: Alana Jordan / Pixabay

A key concept in the psychoanalytic tradition was catharsis. Breuer and Freud defined this as “the process of reducing or eliminating a complex by recalling it to conscious awareness and allowing it to be expressed.”[1] Over many subsequent years, this concept appears to have morphed into the popular assumption that it's “good to emote.” Repression of feeling was thought to keep us locked in mental ill-health, while the expression of feelings could release us into well-being.

This general acceptance that eliciting emotion is of itself therapeutic has been challenged in the past few decades among those working to understand trauma (for example, Babette Rothschild’s emphasis on the need to “titrate” the powerful emotional reactions of trauma-sufferers [2]). This insight has not yet spread throughout the whole field of counselling and psychotherapy practice, even though trauma lies at the core of such work. This is illustrated in the following example:

Richard had joined a long-standing therapeutic group and was in his second session. He shared something about his experiences in a relationship which triggered another member’s distress. This member went into a meltdown, crying, interspersed with a vitriolic personal attack on him, and shouting that she didn’t want him in the group. Richard was completely bemused; he had no idea what had provoked such an attack. He felt as if he had been punched in the stomach. He did not know how to respond. He really wanted the group therapist to give him some support, but the therapist froze, as did the rest of the group. Eventually, the therapist tried to regulate the member’s outburst, but Richard was completely ignored. He left that evening shaken and feeling really isolated.

Richard very nearly didn’t go back to the group. A sense of dread came when it was time for the next session, but he pushed through and brought up in the group how he had been left feeling and told the angry member that he thought it had been a completely unwarranted personal attack. This member replied that this was what the group was for, and if he couldn’t take it, he shouldn’t be in the group. The therapist did not comment.

This group appears to be based on the principle that emotional expression is always good, regardless of the emotions. This approach is by no means unusual, and many therapy training courses provide experiential groups for personal development which are conducted similarly.

In groups with no structure or agenda, where the leader or facilitator does not guide the work but occasionally gives enigmatic interpretations of what is happening, a silent start and lack of direction normally elicit anxiety. In this context, the fear system can activate very powerfully, resulting in attacks, alliances, dominant-submissive behaviours, tensions and silences, leaving people frightened and confused. Emotions are definitely elicited, but whether this is therapeutic is another matter.

article continues after advertisement

If we look at this from a fear system perspective, knowing that fear responses shut down our ability to reflect, to explore and to relate socially, I would suggest that when we think of eliciting emotions, we need to differentiate between fear-based emotions such as anxiety, rage, panic and depression, and socially based emotions such as concern, sadness, loss, affection and gratitude.

We may need to start by regulating fear-based emotions to create sufficient safety for our cognitive and social systems to operate fully; therapy is not possible without the ability to relate or to think reflectively. Emotional expression can become therapeutic when we have first built a safe context.

An example of such a safe context comes from my own experience as a member of a group run according to the McCluskey model of group work [3].

As the group facilitator was finishing a piece of work with one of the members, I made a clumsy intervention which provoked an angry attack on me from another group member; my behaviour had triggered memories of her dominant father.

The facilitator immediately intervened, cutting short the angry attack, pointing out to the angry member that the issue belonged to her to resolve, not to me, and offering her some time to explore her anger towards her father. This was agreed, but before commencing this piece of work, the facilitator turned to me, reiterated that this was not my issue, and offered me some time afterwards to process my previous intervention. In the meantime, aware that I was shaken by the angry attack, the facilitator asked another group member sitting next to me to keep an eye on me and help me to stay connected to the group.

I had been shamed by the attack, and gone into fear collapse, so it was very hard to hear anything or take it in, and I kept drifting off into a dissociated state, but each time I felt myself detaching from the group, I only had to look over to the member beside me, and her warm and welcoming eye contact brought me back into a sense of connectedness which eventually pulled me out of my collapse.

This particular group session taught me a great deal about how fear affected my ability to think and stay connected, because the facilitator’s regulation of fear responses created a safe place in which I could reflect on the effect of fear as I was experiencing it. I therefore disagree with the assumption that it is ‘good to emote.’ Only when emotion is elicited in safety can we hope for a therapeutic outcome. While this has been an underlying principle of trauma work for some time now, I think that this understanding should be applied to the whole field of psychological therapy, as trauma underlies all of our therapeutic work.

item.title: Suicide Prevention Must Include Discussions About Sextortion
item.description:
Adolescence

Suicide Prevention Must Include Discussions About Sextortion

Sextortion is a growing crime with children targeted at much younger ages.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Sextortion frequently starts online and can escalate quickly.
  • Kids are often afraid to seek help, and feelings of shame and desperation can lead to suicidal ideation.
  • Talking to kids about sextortion can help prevent victimization and teach kids how to respond to a problem.
Source: Gemini/Google

September is National Suicide Prevention Month, which can serve as a good opportunity to raise awareness among children, teens, and young people about the risks of sextortion. Sextortion is a form of blackmail where a perpetrator convinces a victim to share explicit images or videos and then threatens to distribute those materials more publicly unless the victim complies with ultimatums, which are commonly demands for additional images, money, or sex. The FBI has warned that sextortion is a rapidly growing crime. Kids can certainly be targeted by people whom they know in real life; however, they are often approached online through social media, messaging platforms, gaming platforms, and even video conferencing platforms. Sextortion tends to escalate quickly and can ensnare children much younger than adults may realize. One study of young people found that more than half of victims were threatened within two weeks of first contact with a perpetrator, and a quarter of that group were threatened during their very first point of contact. Furthermore, one quarter of these victims were 13 years old or younger when they were sextorted (Thorn, 2019).

While the blackmail of a child might have been a rare event 20 or 30 years ago, that is no longer the case. This is not a fringe risk, but rather something that all kids need to be aware of. Sextortion can happen to kids who are well-adjusted, good students, and close to their families. When it occurs, kids feel embarrassed and ashamed. They are often afraid to seek help and feel trapped, panicked, and alone. Unfortunately, these feelings can lead to thoughts of suicide, with a recent study demonstrating a statistically significant relationship between experiencing sextortion and suicidality (Patchin and Hinduja, 2026). This is why talking to kids about sextortion is so important.

The best way to protect kids from sextortion is to limit and closely supervise their online activities. Children should never be communicating with strangers online or sharing explicit imagery with anyone. But if kids don’t follow these online ground rules and end up in a troubling encounter, they still need to know how to respond. Children should understand that the adults in their lives know that sextortion can happen to good kids and that they won’t be blamed or shamed if they find themselves victimized and seek help. They should know to stop all contact with whoever is targeting them and obtain assistance from an adult. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children and the FBI have online resources to help parents and families know how to respond to sextortion and report the crime.

Online victimization is going to be a traumatic and stressful ordeal for anyone to endure. But without prior education, young people have little life experience and perspective to know they are not the first to experience it, and that they should talk to an adult about it. While the victimization itself is distressing, it is the subsequent shame, isolation, and desperation that can do even greater damage and lead to suicidal thoughts. Providing young people with information about sextortion hopefully reduces the likelihood that they become victims by teaching them what to look out for and how to stay safe. But it is equally important to provide anticipatory guidance so that kids know how to respond if they are victimized and understand that they should seek help because sextortion is a fixable problem; they do not need to face it alone.

item.title: Why Missing One Day Makes You Want to Quit
item.description:
Conscientiousness

Why Missing One Day Makes You Want to Quit

What all-or-nothing thinking has to do with your personality.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Low conscientiousness and high emotional sensitivity often combine to make one missed day feel like failure.
  • All-or-nothing thinking tends to treat one missed day as evidence that the whole effort has failed.
  • Resuming after a slip, rather than “starting over,” is often what allows a personality trait to shift.

A client of mine came to our session frustrated. She'd been working on getting more exercise, had been tracking her streak on a fitness app for two weeks, and then missed a Monday because she stayed up too late the night before. She told me she hadn't gone back since. That was three weeks ago.

"Might as Well" Logic

This pattern shows up across a lot of different behaviors. I missed one workout, so I might as well skip the week. I had one drink, so I might as well have five. I went over my budget on Tuesday, so the rest of the month is a wash.

Here's the logic. If the goal was an unbroken streak and the streak is broken, the goal is unattainable now. Moreover, for many people, slipping up can retroactively make previous efforts feel worthless.

Streak trackers can actually accelerate this process for some people. While the visual chain of check marks can be motivating, that glaring empty box has the opposite effect.

What Your Personality Has to Do With It

There are two personality traits that tend to show up in people who get caught in this all-or-nothing pattern.

The first is lower conscientiousness. Conscientiousness is the Big Five trait most associated with self-discipline and follow-through. People lower in conscientiousness often find it hard to maintain habits without external structure, which may be why streak trackers seem alluring at first. But if the behavior hasn't become rewarding or meaningful on its own, missing a day can remove much of what was keeping it going.

The second is higher emotional sensitivity, sometimes called neuroticism. Emotional sensitivity refers to how frequently and intensely you experience distress, and it varies considerably from person to person. When breaking a streak feels distressing, all-or-nothing thinking can kick in. When you're higher in emotional sensitivity, it is easier to go from "I skipped the gym yesterday" to "I'm someone who can't follow through." And then your brain attempts to find relief from discomfort by telling you things like "If I don't restart, I won't feel bad when I inevitably fail again."

The good news is that traits can shift by making deliberate changes to your patterns of thinking and behavior.

Getting Back on Track

The most useful thing you can do after a slip is also the least glamorous one. Simply get back on the horse.

This is no easy feat because it requires sitting with the imperfection of an interrupted record. The streak is gone. The app will show a gap. And if you're higher in emotional sensitivity, you're likely to feel real shame or sadness.

Remind yourself that the streak isn't really the goal. The behavior is. And the behavior is still available on Tuesday even if you missed Monday.

For people lower in conscientiousness, it can help to scaffold the behaviors you're hoping to maintain that are less likely to collapse after one miss. Maybe you enlist a friend to work out with you. Or, you design lighter workouts for "I don't feel like working out" days. If you have to track, maybe track something harder to break, like the number of workouts in the past 30 days.

I'm the Type of Person

Over time, getting back on track becomes easier. If conscientiousness is your challenge, the behavior you're trying to build starts to become reinforcing in its own right, making you more likely to do it again. If neuroticism is getting in the way, each time you get back on the horse gives you evidence that you can tolerate the disappointment or frustration of falling short and keep going anyway. As you maintain these changes, you're not just building a habit; you're actively changing the personality traits that underlie it.

item.title: What Do Digital Breadcrumbs Reveal About Your Mental Health?
item.description:
Social Media

What Do Digital Breadcrumbs Reveal About Your Mental Health?

Algorithms can detect mental health patterns. But who gets to interpret them?

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Machine-learning systems can detect signs of mental health conditions from our digital activity.
  • An algorithm may identify a pattern without understanding the broader living system and influences shaping it.
  • The challenge may be protecting the boundary around what others are permitted to infer.

Almost 80 years have passed since George Orwell published his classic science fiction novel that imagined a dystopian threat to privacy by a controlling government that maintained constant monitoring of its citizens—along with imposing personalized tortures of a person’s greatest nightmare when they did not conform. Orwell depicted the frightening future to take place just over 30 years after the book’s birth: 1984.

Looking at his life, it may not have been such a strange prediction, as he lived through World War I, the Great Depression, and then World War II, which had officially ended a few years before he drafted the book. Not only did Orwell witness and survive recurring patterns of war and suffering, but he also saw the atrocities grow larger and more destructive.

For instance, when WWI ended on November 11, 1918, in the 11th hour, people celebrated Armistice Day and called it “the war to end all wars.” But the Great Depression followed a decade later. And an even greater war, WWII, kicked off a decade after that—and culminated in horrors unimaginable and two atomic bombs that revealed we could decimate entire populations—and destroy the planet while doing it.

Looking at the events of Orwell’s life, it can be easier to infer how he could imagine a government so frightening and controlling. We can all play pseudo-psychologist when we read books or watch movies and wonder what the writer was thinking or ponder their state of mind. Sometimes a person has a more inside scoop to the person, like the Disney producer, Don Hahn, who made the connection to Walt Disney’s mother’s death and the recurring theme of deceased mothers in many Disney films.

Part of a writer’s life—and anyone famous—knows they hold their life, motivation, relationships, and sometimes their mental health to public scrutiny and chatter. It’s a little heartbreaking, and having worked with some people in the spotlight, I know all too well the mental health burden that the invasion of privacy, mob mentality, and stalking behaviors can have.

But what happens when you are not famous?

Today we are seeing a new threat to privacy with social media and the digital breadcrumbs we leave behind in comments on various platforms, including artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots. This includes young people and old, across borders and cultures.

Most people have a general understanding that algorithms are tracking them, learning their preferences, and showing them targeted advertisements. I have heard more than one young person say they love that because they don’t have to wade through things that don’t interest them and feel like the targeted ads are like a personalized shopper.

But what happens when the machines begin monitoring and diagnosing your mental health?

This isn't science fiction. Researchers have been developing machine-learning systems capable of identifying signs associated with mental health conditions from people's digital activity for years. In a 2025 systematic review, Rizaldi et al. examined 40 studies using machine learning and natural-language processing to detect conditions including depression, anxiety, stress, posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), suicidal ideation, eating disorders, and obsessive-compulsive disorder from data that included social media and digital posts. The researchers also identified continuing problems involving validation, labeling, and generalizability across populations and platforms.

A newer 2026 scoping review by He et al. looked at 136 studies from 2021 to January 2026 that examined mental health detection risks from social media text and pointed out that most of the research identified a proxy-based risk rather than a clinical diagnosis—which means patterns of risk were identified, not a clinical diagnosis.

But patterns aren't promises. Human behavior does not occur in a vacuum. The environments we inhabit shape what we say, how we say it, and even what parts of ourselves we present (hello, selfies that have become increasingly normalized). A trained clinician can consider the context that might be shaping the pattern while also looking at the person’s history and culture, and ask the person what is happening in their life.

An algorithm may identify a pattern without understanding the broader living system and influences shaping a pattern.

And yet what happens when people treat the pattern data as the whole?

Bigger questions are: Who gets access to this information, and what risks come to the person who has been marked as a mental health risk? And what happens when an algorithm infers a mental health risk that a person has never disclosed, sought treatment for, or perhaps even recognized themselves? What protections apply to information that is neither a formal diagnosis nor something the individual knowingly revealed?

Beneath these questions is another powerful one: Where should the boundary lie between what we reveal and what others are permitted to infer?

Because many of us have learned the power of boundaries with a difficult relationship. Or boundaries between work and time off.

But technology is increasingly erasing boundaries.

Consider the changing boundaries around public and private information. Between what I have communicated and what you have inferred. Between my time plugged in and my time unplugged. And now, between what I know about myself and what an algorithm believes about me—and how it may be supporting me or surveilling me.

What makes a boundary healthy isn't simply that it exists. It's what the boundary is protecting—and what it still allows to pass through.

When Orwell imagined rigid surveillance imposed by a powerful government watching its citizens, I doubt he could have imagined billions of ordinary people voluntarily paying for surveillance with smartphones in their pockets (or glued to their eyes). Nor would he have guessed that people would catalog their daily activities or share their most intimate and vulnerable moments with a machine that is tracking and influencing them in ways research has barely scratched.

Orwell's imagined world asked what might happen when surveillance gave powerful institutions unprecedented access to people's lives.

Nearly 80 years later, we face a different version of that question. Our digital breadcrumbs can increasingly reveal—or lead machines to infer—things we never consciously disclosed.

The challenge may no longer be simply protecting what we choose to keep private. It may be protecting the boundary around what others are permitted to infer.

item.title: Your College Student Still Needs You, Just Differently
item.description:
Academic Problems and Skills

Your College Student Still Needs You, Just Differently

Three shifts can help your child build judgment, relationships, and resilience.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • College gives young adults a chance to practice independence while support is still available.
  • Solving problems for college students can keep them from building confidence in their own judgment.
  • Building their own support network teaches students how to seek help and form meaningful relationships.
  • Managing their own responsibilities and setbacks helps students build independence and resilience.

“College is exciting but now I need to learn to survive.” said Sabrina, an incoming first-year college student. I could sense the anxiety and excitement in her voice. She wanted to be independent to make her own decisions. Yet, she also realized all the responsibilities she would have to take on.

I want to focus on what parents go through this transition. For nearly two decades, you may have helped architect the conditions for your child’s success, but when college begins, that responsibility shifts to them.

As a professor and leadership coach, I believe that college provides a valuable period of supported independence. While students have greater freedom, they also have a vast support system including access to academic advisors, health services, and counseling. Here are three shifts you can make to support their transition.

1. From Architect to Thinking Partner

If your adult child texts you with a problem, what do you do? If your tendency is to solve it, don't! When you start the conversation, consider asking them: “What have you tried so far?” “How did that approach work for you?” “What information might you be missing?” If another person is involved, ask, “How might they see the situation?” or “What do you think they expect from you?” Then help your child explore options without choosing for them.

The goal is to teach them problem-solving skills so that they gain confidence in their own abilities. Helping them think through the situation builds judgment they can use when facing a challenge in the future.

Your experience still matters. There will be times when your advice is exactly what they need. The shift is to make advice less automatic. Before giving them the answer, give them the opportunity to find one.

2. From Creating Connections to Helping Them Build a Network

Before college, much of your child’s community was structured around them. You chose schools, arranged activities, coordinated transportation, encouraged sports and clubs, and created opportunities for them to meet other people.

College changes that. This is where students need to develop social initiative, relationship-building, and help-seeking. Your role is to encourage those behaviors without creating the connections for them. Instead of researching clubs for them, ask, “Where could you meet people who share your interests?” If they are struggling, ask, “Who at school could help you with this?” One question can tell you a great deal: “Who would you go to if you needed help?”

article continues after advertisement

Learning how to build a healthy support system is a skill they will need again when they start a job, move to a new city, or face another major transition.

3. From Managing the System to Helping Them Build Their Own

A college student can be academically talented and still struggle because they have never had to create their own support systems. Freedom exposes where someone else was providing structure. Increasing their resilience will be essential for their academic success.

When you start the conversation, consider asking questions that encourage reflection:

“What system are you using to keep track of your deadlines?” “What did you learn from how you prepared for this exam?” “What broke down?” and “What will you do differently next time?”

If your child misses a deadline and you begin reminding them about every future deadline, you have become the system again. If you help them understand why they missed it and create a better approach, they are learning to manage themselves.

Know When to Step Back and When to Step In

Of course, giving your child more autonomy does not mean ignoring serious problems. If your child is experiencing significant emotional distress, an inability to function, or safety concerns, you may need to step in and may require professional support.

A useful distinction is between discomfort and distress. Discomfort often calls for coaching. Distress may call for intervention. Giving them room to struggle does not mean disappearing. It means making a more deliberate choice about the kind of support they need.

article continues after advertisement

Transfer the Capability, Not Just the Responsibility

For years, you have provided more than love and support. You have provided strategy, structure, resources, motivation, persistence, and judgment. College begins the gradual transfer of those capabilities.

That transfer happens through hundreds of small moments. Do you provide the answer or help them find it? Do you build the structure or help them create one? Do you prevent the mistake or help them learn from it?

This transition requires something from parents, too. Sometimes you will have to watch your child struggle with something you know how to solve. You may have to accept that they will make decisions you would not make yourself.

Your role is not disappearing. Your role is simply evolving. Your college child still needs you.

item.title: Why, and How, to Build a More Transparent Relationship
item.description:
Fantasies

Why, and How, to Build a More Transparent Relationship

Transparency can bring you and your partner closer. Here's how to approach it with care.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Relational transparency builds trust by demystifying one's partner and reducing defensiveness.
  • Both partners should discuss readiness and needs before increasing transparency.
  • Transparency requires discernment—share with care, not as total disclosure.

Transparency is revealing your emotions, thoughts, and choices to your partner. Transparency can help both of you to become more human in your relationship. Feeling vulnerable, lost, and scared becomes a humanizing expression for each person.

Source: The Jopwell Collection/Unsplash

This is especially helpful in building trust. Typically, transparency demystifies your partner. This lets you see who you’re choosing, who you’re believing, and who you’re trusting. The more transparency becomes a relationship norm, the less guarded and defensive you become, and the less pretense you carry.

Preparing to Be More Transparent

Depending on how much transparency is currently in your relationship, moving toward more can be a minor adjustment or a significant one. Let’s assume it will be more than a minor modification. If so, here are some steps to support greater transparency.

  • Become more self-transparent. Take regular inventory of your emotions and the stories you carry about yourself, your partner, and life in general.
  • Inventory with compassion. The more you can hold your emotions and stories with compassion, the more comfort you’ll have self-disclosing.
  • Practice. It may be helpful to become more transparent with a friend, mentor, or sibling. We choose to be transparent with someone because we want them to see us. Transparency comes more easily when it’s part of your lifestyle, not just a way to relate to your significant other.
  • Let your partner know you intend to be more transparent. It’s always helpful to speak about an upcoming change in a relationship rather than simply implementing it. Let your partner know what you might need from them, such as acceptance, empathy, and curiosity.
  • Ask your partner if they feel ready to experience more of you. If they’re not sure, invite them to tell you how they feel when you are more transparent.
  • Ask your partner if they feel ready to be more transparent. If they feel ready, ask them what they need from you as they do so. If they’re not ready, decide if you want to go ahead anyway.

Receiving More Transparency

More transparency can bring a relationship more understanding and depth. Like any act of growth, old ways fall away as new ones take their place. Even if it’s a good thing, a new level of transparency may bring some tension. Here are some suggestions for when you hear your partner being more transparent.

article continues after advertisement
  • Remain grounded. Deep breathing, feeling the floor or chair beneath you, and noticing one or two internal sensations in your body. It might be tightness or pulsations of energy. The key is to not react.
  • Listen reflectively with empathy. Simply say back what you hear. “Sounds like you feel a deep loss with Peter leaving the team.” Or, “I’m hearing you don’t yet feel comfortable in your new position.”
  • Notice how you’re feeling when hearing your partner’s disclosure. You may feel glad, sad, angry, or scared. Give yourself permission to express your emotions after your partner has finished speaking.
  • Avoid offering any criticism or disparaging remarks. Not everything you hear will feel wonderful. However, it can be an opportunity to work with diversity as you accept your partner’s uniqueness.

Transparency Calls for Discernment

Being transparent does not mean revealing everything transpiring in your emotional world or in your varied thoughts. It does mean being discerning about what’s in your best interest, your partner’s welfare, and the relationship’s. Here are some suggestions for guiding your discernment.

  • Fantasies. I don’t recommend disclosing your sexual fantasies about others unless you're planning to act on one or such sharing is a norm in your relationship.
  • Forgiveness. Avoid using transparency to seek your partner’s forgiveness, as it can easily disrupt your partner’s honest response. Work on forgiving yourself.
  • Psychological or medical challenges facing your partner. If your partner is facing emotional stress or a medical situation, consider postponing your transparency.
  • Truth and compassion. We don’t consider the option of too much compassion in a verbal exchange. However, how much truth you share always deserves discretion. One question to ask: Am I typically overprotective of my partner? If the answer is “Yes,” then your partner may be able to handle more truth than you give them credit for. If your partner is accustomed to a wide range of transparency, they may also be ready to hear a deeper truth.
  • Roles reversed. If the roles were reversed and your partner was about to tell you what you’re getting ready to reveal, would you want to hear such a message? If the response is “No," then seriously consider withholding your disclosure.
article continues after advertisement

A commitment to transparency is a wonderful way to get more authentic in a relationship. However, transparency without discernment can unleash suppressed resentment and anger.

The purpose of transparency is to disclose what you believe can serve each of you and your relationship. I encourage you to notice any urgency to be transparent, which may be driven by a hidden agenda. Take your time. Let the urgency subside and share your truth when you can engage in a more relaxed process.

Of course, talking about betrayal may be the hardest thing to be transparent about. It helps if the recipient is less self-righteous, not enamored with I would never do anything like that. And it also helps if both parties have released their relationship from the idyllic hold of “betrayal can’t happen here.”

item.title: The Decomposition of Intelligence
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Decomposition of Intelligence

AI may be revealing that intelligence was never one thing to begin with.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • AI may separate capabilities that human cognition tightly integrates.
  • Broad AI ability may not be organized the way human intelligence is.
  • AI may reveal that our definition of intelligence is too human.
Source: hainguyenrp / Pixabay

Almost 2 years ago, I wrote about an idea called anti-intelligence. In this post, I wasn't suggesting that artificial intelligence (AI) was unintelligent or that it resulted in some adverse impact on human thinking. I was trying to describe a process that felt, at least to me, upside down or inverted. While AI could generate smart language and solve tough problems, it accomplished this without the qualities we associate with a human mind. At the core of my idea was that AI's output looked familiar, but its computational process didn't. In many ways, AI's computation—a stateless, pattern-based, and high-dimensional construct—was weird, disconnected, and perhaps even "alien" as some today suggest.

At that time, I saw anti-intelligence as a way of describing the differences between human intelligence and AI's techno-computation. In a word, it was different. Not better or worse, but fundamentally different. Human thought comes from a life shaped by our lived experiences. AI seemed to reproduce many of the artifacts of our cognition, but without a process that came close to being human.

I think that's still true. But I've started to wonder if anti-intelligence was revealing something more, something about intelligence itself.

The Curious Unity of Intelligence

Let's take a step back. Science has spent more than a hundred years studying something called "g," or general intelligence. The idea is fairly simple—our cognitive abilities tend to work together. Someone who performs well on one kind of cognitive test or task is more likely to perform well on another. And this collective cognitive pattern is called the positive manifold. Simply put, human cognition hangs together.

There’s also a curious linguistic coincidence here. Psychology has a g in general intelligence. Artificial general intelligence (AGI) also uses the g word. Both terms come from different perspectives, and suggest a question. What does “general” actually mean in general intelligence?

Let's push on this a little bit more. We usually imagine AGI as intelligence that broadens to include expansive domains, from language to math to computation. But these expanded domains and integration may not be the same thing. Perhaps AI could become highly capable across almost endless domains but without those abilities being organized like the general intelligence of a human mind. The g might be different, and AGI could become "general" without possessing the g in the human sense.

Taking Cognition Apart

Some of the capabilities we associate with human intelligence may actually come from the architecture in which it is formed. And that sentence, curious as it may sound, is worth reading again. The likes of language and reasoning, to name a few, all live inside the same biological organism. They develop and co-exist together, influencing one another from the inside. Remember, they hang together.

article continues after advertisement

AI offers a different case. A large language model (LLM) can correctly answer a difficult problem and then stumble over something that seems simple, if not trivial. Its abilities don't always align with our human understanding of what a "smart mind" is. This computational "jaggedness" also shares a border with another feature I've written about called fragility. Small irregularities in an LLM dialogue can sometimes produce large errors. And this can happen even when the model's performance stays strong elsewhere. In the future, I imagine that this jaggedness will be fixed. And if these capabilities begin to move together—hang together as in a human construct—AI may eventually develop something like its own positive manifold. And that, in and of itself, is interesting.

Key point: Capabilities that once seemed inseparable are becoming separable. We have studied intelligence almost entirely through our human architecture. And for the first time, we have AI to compare ourselves with.

I need to point out that this story began long before AI. Medicine and psychology have been studying this for a long time. Split-brain research has challenged some of our assumptions about the unity of mind. We've seen cognition come apart. And today, AI may allow us to watch aspects of it being assembled separately.

This is where anti-intelligence still feels relevant to me. AI may be separating capacities that genuinely belong to intelligence, or it may be building computational analogues that only look familiar from the outside. I don't think we know yet, and it might not even be on the radar screen.

Rethinking Anti-intelligence

When I first started using the term anti-intelligence, I was trying to describe how AI's computational architecture was different from human cognition.

But could it be that what we call intelligence is actually a "cluster of capacities" that science tied together? Those capacities "hang together" in us, so maybe we assumed that their integration was simply what intelligence is. For more than a century, g has described that togetherness. AI may force us to ask what it actually means.

So here's my bold and imposing thought: Perhaps we have mistaken the architecture of human intelligence for the definition of intelligence. And AI is the first chance to "decompose" this construct and learn that intelligence wasn't one thing in the first place.
