item.title: Science vs. Philosophy
item.description:
Philosophy

Science vs. Philosophy

How relevant is science to philosophy?

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • "Naturalism" in philosophy is often vaguely defined and varies widely in interpretation.
  • Radical naturalists argue philosophy should be fully continuous with the sciences.
  • Analytic philosophy’s focus on internal coherence risks letting problematic ideas persist unchallenged.

My last blog posts calling for a scientific turn in philosophy and the abandonment of aprioristic philosophy largely resulted in three responses. There were philosophers who agreed, of course, but the main response was either:

  • This isn’t even a debate. Philosophy is already scientific.

Or:

  • Philosophy should not be scientific.

The philosopher Liam Kofi Bright, whom I previously responded to in an earlier essay, where I argued that naturalistic philosophy can provide us with the optimistic answer to his pessimism about traditional analytic philosophy, noted that he doesn't even encounter philosophy vs. science debates anymore. But is this debate over meta-philosophy really over?

No doubt, among philosophers of science, this debate may seem largely obsolete (it is not). And Bright’s department, the LSE Department of Philosophy, Logic and Scientific Method, is one of the most naturalistic ones in existence. Indeed, their very motto calls for the continuity between philosophy and science:

Because of that mission, I applied and received an offer to pursue a Ph.D. at the LSE, but I decided to go to Sydney, where Paul Griffiths and Peter Godfrey-Smith, as radical naturalists, offered what I saw as the best place to write a thesis in naturalist biological philosophy, with a lab in a biomedical research centre. Nevertheless, I spend part of my Ph.D. as a visiting Ph.D. student at the LSE, so I’m not surprised that Bright doesn’t find this debate even arise in the circles he is in. It’s one of the most naturalistic philosophy departments in the world.

Conceptualizing Naturalism

But, of course, many other philosophers vehemently opposed my call for scientific philosophy, so the debate doesn’t seem over quite yet. In part, the confusion may come down to how one conceptualizes naturalism.

Naturalism, the view that science and philosophy should be continuous with each other, is sometimes said to have become the default view among analytic philosophers. Yet, that is far from true.

Unfortunately, the label of naturalism has become more and more deflated over the years. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on naturalism begins by stating that: “The term 'naturalism' has no very precise meaning in contemporary philosophy.” The naturalist philosopher Owen Flanagan traced dozens of alternative uses.

The weakest level in which one can be a naturalist as a philosopher is to insist that one’s philosophical views are not logically inconsistent with science. But that is not sufficient for those, like myself, who consider themselves radical naturalists. Or, alternatively, genuine naturalists. For the radical naturalists, philosophy must be radically continuous with the sciences, become one with them, much like philosophy was once the term we used for both science and philosophy, before they became culturally, institutionally, and conceptually separated. Some radical naturalists have claimed the label of scientism, once a pejorative, for themselves to avoid this linguistic confusion. And the debate over how science may supplant or replace philosophy is alive and well. Only this month, there was a big discussion on DailyNous (the news platform for philosophers) over whether experimental philosophy really counts as philosophy.

Evidently this debate on the soul of philosophy is far from over. For logical consistency is an incredibly weak criterion. An ingenious philosopher can make almost any set of ideas compatible. Indeed, logical consistency may not be the non plus ultra it is usually taken for.

Unfortunately, there isn’t a great deal of writing about radically naturalistic meta-philosophy out there that I find useful. One of my main philosophical influences, the late Dan Dennett, barely even bothered to write about his meta-philosophy. Luckily, this prompted Don Ross, Andrew Brook, and David L. Thompson to release a volume dedicated to trying to reconstruct it in Dennett’s Philosophy: A Comprehensive Assessment.

Almost all critics of Dennett’s work I’ve encountered over the years did not understand his naturalistic meta-philosophy, which was radically unlike their own. Thankfully, Don Ross offered an excellent explanation for Dennett’s resistance to aprioristic philosophy. He writes:

A philosophical thesis must mainly appeal to the virtue of consistency among beliefs we are already disposed to hold on the basis of experience. Most such beliefs have a property that must be grounds for suspicion to a radical naturalist such as Dennett: They will have been entertained for long enough (at least by somebody) to have grown comfortable. This implies both that they will have settled into our belief corpus through being domesticated by our intuitions, and that they will have had some influence on that corpus through the process of making themselves at home.

This fact about our psychology is rarely acknowledged by analytic philosophers. The very goal of analytic philosophy to strive for logical consistency invites the laundering of bad ideas we’ve culturally inherited, rather than to challenge them.

item.title: No Sex Please, We’re Gen Z*
item.description:
Adolescence

No Sex Please, We’re Gen Z*

Why are adolescents and young adults having less sex?

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Gen Z are experiencing a sex recession.
  • The sex recession can be understood in a wider social/cultural context.
  • Human dating is being replaced by AI companions for some Gen Z.

Barely a week goes by without a disparaging headline about Gen Z. This time, the headlines I've been seeing focus on the assertion that they are having less sex than previous generations did at their age, which is roughly 15 to 29.

Curious to know more, I consulted the premier sex research centre, the Kinsey Institute, which has been researching sex, gender, and relationships for 80 years. Their famous midcentury reports shocked society by revealing that premarital sex and homosexuality were far more common than most people assumed. Are their findings about the sex lives of Gen Z shocking too?

A bit; but for converse reasons. The Kinsey Institute confirms a "sex recession" among young adults, with the number reportedly not having sex in the past year doubling from 12 percent in 2010 to 24 percent in 2024, and 30 percent of 18–29-year-olds reporting having had no sex at all in the past three months.1

But why?

Reasons Gen Z Are Not Having Sex

When this theme shows up in my therapy room, the main reasons Gen Z say they’re not having sex are the same reasons that apply to many of the quirks and challenges they are grappling with—money and tech.

Due to financial constraints, young adults are living with their parents for longer. According to the Office for National Statistics, the average age that people leave home has risen to 28.2 Some move out for university, but many boomerang back, known as “re-nesting.” Living with mum and dad might be good for Gen Z’s finances, but it’s not so good for their sex lives, with 64 percent of those living at home saying they had no sex in the preceding three months due to lack of privacy.1

Finances also get in the way of dating, which gets in the way of sex. My Gen Z clients lament the eye-watering cost of a single night out, which, for many, eats up much of their weekly income, even outside of big cities, where the cost is astronomical. In London, for example, the classic “dinner and a movie” date costs upward of £100, and who can afford that? Even a couple of drinks cost about the same as one hour’s national living wage, which in the UK is £10.85–£12.71 depending on age. Gen Z are dating less and going out less in general, because they can’t afford it.

Role of Technology

Another reason they spend less time socialising in person is that they’re doing it online. According to the Institute for Family Studies, the average time Gen Z spend meeting people offline has fallen from around 13 hours a week in 2010 to just over five in 2024.3

Before we start berating screens (again) and pointing the finger at young people for being antisocial (again), I think we should consider “the COVID effect.” Today’s 15- to 29-year-olds were 9 to 23 during the pandemic lockdowns, when social contact was forbidden and socialising online was the only option. For young to mid-term Gen Z’s, this came at a formative time in their social and emotional development, when many of us learn the rules and risks of dating.

article continues after advertisement

Through absolutely no fault of their own, many learned to fulfil their friendship, intimacy, and, in some cases, sexual needs through technology. According to the Kinsey Institute, roughly 25 percent of young adults say that social media and artificial intelligence (AI) meet their intimacy needs, while 28 percent say that screen time reduces their motivation to seek in-person sexual connections.1 Put simply, they’re just not that into it.

But what about the ones who are—why aren’t they having sex? Again, it’s partly due to technology. If smartphone surveillance, digital trackers, and the risk of being photographed or filmed were commonplace in the 1980s and early ‘90s, I’m certain my generation would have been having a lot less sex, too. Hyper visibility and online comparing and despairing have also made contemporary adolescents hypersensitive to rejection. Dating and sex have always carried risks, but pre-Gen Z there was no possibility of bad dates or messy sex being recorded and nonconsensually shared in public domains.

But what if the risk of rejection, heartbreak, and nonconsensual image sharing could be avoided? What if there was an intimate partner who would always be available and interested, always complementary, always validating, always willing to meet your every emotional need? Enter the AI companion. According to one study, 72 percent of Gen Z have interacted with an AI companion, and 49 percent have formed a “meaningful relationship.”4 Technology is also on hand (pardon the pun) to meet Gen Z’s sexual needs, with around three-quarters accessing online pornography regularly, 43 percent accessing it weekly, and 19 percent accessing it daily.5

article continues after advertisement

So, what if Gen Z are having less sex? I think that rather than pointing fingers of blame or dismissing the “sex recession” as something trivial, we need to consider the facts within broader social and cultural contexts in an effort to understand what modern life is like for young adults. And the only way we can do that is by being comfortable enough and open enough to talk about sex—no matter how much, how often, and in what form it’s showing up.

*The title of this piece is borrowed from a 1973 British comedy, "No Sex Please, We're British."

item.title: Why We Read Novels
item.description:
Imagination

Why We Read Novels

Novels can be read for not only for pleasure but to improve our mental health.

Posted September 28, 2026

You can even read after hanging up your bathing suits!
Source: Jenni Ogden

The joys of reading novels

It’s been a while since I wrote a post for this blog—eight years, in fact. My last was titled “Moving On,” and here I still am, moved on and coming back. In those eight years, I have continued to live with my husband on an off-grid island 100km off the northeast coast of Aotearoa New Zealand, and have continued to write novels and have gone backward rather than forward when it comes to learning how to write them.

The more years that pass, the more workshops I do (mostly as a student, sometimes as the teacher) and, on the plus side, the more novels I read. My old blog posts were about “brains, books and being happy,” but the focus of my new posts will be mainly novels (by both women and men, many recent publications but some published years ago) and why reading them is good for us, from the point of view of someone who is interested in psychology, mental health, well-being, and happiness. All of us, I hope!

I belong to NetGalley, a platform where publishers and authors upload advance reader copies (ARCs) of their books and audiobooks (fiction and nonfiction) months before they are published, and members can request them. If their request is granted, it is hoped that they will review the book and post their review on as many platforms as possible (Goodreads, Amazon, etc.). Any avid reader can register as a reader or reviewer member of NetGalley. There is also a UK branch. So far, I have reviewed 318 books, which marks me as an active member and gives me “Professional Reader” status. Now I often receive e-mails from publishers asking if they can send me a digital ARC.

But, of course, I also purchase many books myself because I am addicted. If I read a great review or listen to one of the excellent author interview podcasts available—the UK Waterstones podcast is my favorite—while walking our beach, AirPods allowing me to also hear the sea and the birds perfectly clearly, I’ll likely have the book on my Kindle that same day. Like many readers, I love print books, and my study, where I am writing this, is also our library (photo above).

Public libraries are precious, but not everyone has a library nearby. Living here and reading as many books as I do, if I purchased every book in its printed form, we may have to sell our house, and then where would we put them all? Also, books published in the U.S. or UK can take a long time to make it into NZ bookstores. So I admit, I love my Kindle.

I don’t think it matters how you consume a book: print, e-book, or audiobook. It is still a book. E-books tend to be much cheaper and thus less likely to be a barrier to those with less money. That can only be good.

And for the author, it is far better to have a thousand readers than 20. One of the arguments of traditional publishers is that purchasing print books will provide the author with more money. This is often not true. The royalty rate an author gets on an e-book is usually much higher than on a print book, as the surge in successful self-published authors who make a living from their books attests.

So why do we read novels, or if we don’t (perhaps because we don’t have time), why might we try to fit reading a novel more frequently into our days—or nights? First and foremost, we read novels for pleasure, pure and simple. A way to escape for a while, or a way to relax yourself to sleep. So don’t feel every novel has to be more than that.

article continues after advertisement

But often the novel we can’t put down or continue to think about long after we have reluctantly closed the book is a story that draws us into the minds of the characters, helping us to feel what they feel, perhaps echoing feelings and situations we have experienced in the past or are experiencing in our current lives. This empathy that we feel is perhaps the most remarkable “emotion” that stories can foster. That the written word can be such a powerful stimulus for empathy depends on the reader’s ability to imagine those worlds and the characters and their lives that are described on the page. (And the author’s ability to turn their own imagination into words.)

When we watch a TV drama, our imaginations don’t have to do so much work; many of you will know how easy it is to tear up when someone on the screen cries, even more so if it is the news and a real story. But perhaps a written story can be even more powerful because we can read it at our own pace and stop and reflect on it.

Becoming immersed in a story told from the perspective of someone completely outside of our own experience helps us understand diverse perspectives. Historical novels can immerse us in a past era, while science fiction can immerse us in the future. Funny stories that make us laugh, especially those gems that result in fits of giggles, have multiple positive effects on our bodies and mental health. Fully engaged laughter, the sort you couldn’t suppress if you tried, has been linked to about a 30 percent reduction in cortisol, a hormone related to stress. Laughter also releases feel-good brain chemicals like dopamine and serotonin.

Novels that we find difficult to stop thinking about, the ones we want to talk about with our friends and book clubs, are the stories that challenge or support our belief systems, provoke discussion, and sometimes change our behavior. They are the novels that we learn from; fictional characters who find ways to cope with shame or loneliness, loss or grief, can show us new ways that, in time, we too might try. And characters don’t have to be human; they can be a dog or a horse or ET. But human characters, animals, and aliens whose feelings we can empathize with aren’t the only ways a well-told story can evoke empathy or grief. I have found myself in tears when reading a story about a dying coral reef.

article continues after advertisement

I have in my previous posts often written about books, including this one on bibliotherapy. This is a practice where, following an in-depth clinical assessment by a highly trained bibliotherapist (not me!), specific books are then prescribed for the client to read, with the intention of enriching and inspiring the client, as well as speaking to their special problems.

Even better, read on a beach. This is the beach where I live, walk, and read.
Source: Jenni Ogden

In each new post after this introductory one, I will take one novel (or occasionally a nonfiction book that has empathy at its heart) that I have rated 5/5 and, without of course revealing too much about the story, look at how a reader might learn something about themselves and their own lives and interactions and emotions by thinking about or like those fictional characters. Perhaps I’ll also venture into the emotional and psychological ups and downs of writing fiction. I’ll post my first book blog in a few days, and after that I’ll aim to post once a month, featuring a different book in each blog. At first, most of these will be those sorts of novels book clubs love to read because they raise interesting discussion questions. These can of course cover a wide range: contemporary, historical, cozy mysteries, literary fiction, even thrillers! Hopefully, you will find some novels to read along the way.

I hope we connect again soon through our mutual love of novels! Thank you for reading.

item.title: Hybrid Flourishing: What Should Progress Mean After 2030?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Hybrid Flourishing: What Should Progress Mean After 2030?

Beyond coping to thriving amid artificial intelligence.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Generative AI reshapes how we work, learn, communicate, and create, while adding pressure on natural systems.
  • Flourishing depends on whether people retain the ability and volition to think, choose, and contribute.
  • Global frameworks organise collective action, yet hybrid flourishing is also shaped through ordinary choices.
Hybrid flourishing is the cause and consequence of social, ecological, economic, and technological dynamics.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT, 2026

For much of modern history, progress has been described through largely linear measures. Economies should grow. People should live longer and healthier lives. Poverty should fall. Societies should become safer, fairer, and more prosperous. Yet human life is multidimensional. Economic growth can coexist with inequality and environmental degradation; technological sophistication can deepen isolation and weaken social cohesion; material prosperity can erode the ecological foundations on which it depends. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) intensifies these dynamics, reshaping how we work, learn, communicate, create, and decide while adding pressure on natural systems.

The 2026 Planetary Health Check found that seven of nine planetary boundaries have been transgressed. Meanwhile, the OECD’s 2026 measurement roadmap argues that treating the “digital economy” as a separate sphere is obsolete. Yet AI is still discussed at technology conferences, growth at economic forums, inequality in social policy debates, and climate at environmental summits. Human beings do not experience life in separate rooms. We inhabit these systems simultaneously, and our experiences and expressions shape them in return. This is where hybrid flourishing begins.

One life, four interconnected systems

Consider an ordinary decision to use an AI assistant at work. It can save time, change how we think and which skills we practise, increase productivity, and add demand for computing infrastructure. That infrastructure requires capital, electricity, water, minerals, and land. Investment decisions affect communities and ecosystems; those conditions influence markets, politics, and individual choices. Follow almost any thread far enough, and it meets the others.

Society, ecology, economy, and technology form an interacting system shaped by human experience and expression. We create technologies from our aspirations, values, and incentives; those technologies influence how we communicate and decide. Economic choices reshape incentives and opportunities. We depend on nature for food, water, energy, health, and stability while transforming it through production and consumption. Society forms us, while our actions reproduce or change it. Flourishing emerges from this continuous exchange between people and their environments.

What does hybrid flourishing mean?

Hybrid flourishing is the capacity of individuals and communities to thrive amid uncertainty in environments shaped by technological evolution, ecological stress, social disruption, and economic inequality.

First, flourishing is a capacity, rather than a static condition. Income, education, healthcare, security, and a healthy environment remain essential, while flourishing also depends on whether people retain the ability and volition to think, choose, and contribute. Agency is therefore a nexus of meaningful development.

article continues after advertisement

Second, flourishing must be possible within uncertainty. We cannot wait for technological change to settle, ecological disruption to end, or geopolitics to stabilise. Flourishing involves the capability to navigate change consciously and help shape what comes next.

Third, the forces influencing flourishing must be addressed as interdependent. AI can improve healthcare, education, and climate modelling, while its infrastructure consumes energy, water, land, and materials. Ecological disruption affects health, migration, productivity, and inequality; economic conditions influence who benefits from technology and who bears its costs. A post-2030 agenda therefore needs to pursue the multidimensional well-being of people and planet while accounting explicitly for our evolving relationship with AI.

Fourth, hybrid flourishing starts from the inside out and is nurtured from the outside in. It is the cause and consequence of human mindsets and external conditions that are mutually supportive.

Living in the Hybrid Tipping Zone

We are navigating a Hybrid Tipping Zone: a period in which natural intelligence, AI, and the social, economic, and planetary systems surrounding them are changing one another sufficiently to alter the trajectory of human development.

Human agency shows why this matters. Experimenting with AI can expand capability; integration can save time and broaden access to knowledge. Yet integration can gradually become reliance. When we repeatedly outsource writing, remembering, analysing, or deciding, we change the conditions under which those capacities develop, creating a vulnerability to decay. At scale, the effects travel outward: schools redesign learning, employers restructure jobs, labour markets reward different skills, capital flows toward digital infrastructure, and energy systems respond to new demand. People adapt their aspirations and behaviour accordingly. Technological change becomes social, economic, ecological, and deeply personal.

The Hybrid Tipping Zone therefore raises two questions that belong together: What direction is the whole system taking, and who are we becoming along the way?

Beyond 2030: measuring a hybrid world

Hybrid flourishing becomes especially relevant as attention turns beyond 2030. The Sustainable Development Goals established a shared understanding that poverty, health, education, equality, prosperity, and environmental sustainability are interconnected. The next agenda inherits that insight in a world where human and technological activity are increasingly intertwined.

Hybrid Development Goals could provide an overarching logic for this era by recognising the reciprocal relationship among human experience and expression, society, ecology, economy, and technology. They would ask whether people retain meaningful agency; whether productivity generates shared prosperity; whether technology strengthens human capabilities and communities; whether technological gains respect ecological limits; and whether today’s efficiencies expand tomorrow’s possibilities.

article continues after advertisement

A Hybrid Flourishing Index could provide a corresponding measurement tool, examining whether progress across these systems expands the capacity of people and planet to flourish. It could encompass human agency, social trust, digital dignity, planetary health, equitable capability, and institutional stewardship. Its purpose would be to make consequential dynamics visible rather than compress life into one number. The Index would tell us how we are doing; the Hybrid Tipping Zone asks where we are heading and who we are becoming.

Flourishing starts at home

Global frameworks organise collective action, yet hybrid flourishing is also shaped through ordinary choices. Four questions offer a practical starting point:

  1. Agency: Am I using technology to strengthen my judgment or surrender it?
  2. Capability: Is it helping me learn and do more while retaining capacities worth keeping?
  3. Connection: What does this choice contribute to my relationships and ability to participate?
  4. Conditions: What social, economic, and ecological conditions does it reinforce—for me, others, and those who come after us?

A prompt seems intangible until we remember the data centre. A purchase seems economic until we follow its materials and labour. An investment seems financial until we consider what it enables. A convenience seems personal until millions adopt it and institutions reorganise around the resulting behaviour.

Our experiences become expressions; expressions become patterns; patterns become systems; and systems return to shape human experience. That circularity is the heart of hybrid flourishing. The task is to recognise the systems we are part of, preserve our capacity to choose within them, and use that agency to create conditions in which everyone, present and future, has a fair chance to flourish in harmony with nature.

item.title: Envy Is Never About the Other Person
item.description:
Jealousy

Envy Is Never About the Other Person

Four films show how envy reveals our shadow side and what we secretly want.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Envy grows out of social comparison, and what we envy often points to what we believe we lack.
  • The same pang of envy can signal an unmet need, a clash of values, or a hidden fear of failing.
  • Envy often traces back to early attachment, sibling rivalry, or families that prized achievement.

Envy is rooted in social comparison. An envious individual compares their own status, abilities, or possessions to those of others, and this comparison can take many forms. For example, are you feeling envious of someone you don’t know on Instagram because you don’t think they deserve to be on vacation? Are you feeling envy toward a billionaire because you don’t think they deserve their wealth? Do you feel envious when your best friend gets a promotion? These are all different scenarios of envy. The first might make you realize you need a vacation. The second may stem from feeling that someone you admire only deserves to be wealthy, so the envy stems from value-based thinking about who gets what. The third is a friend of yours, and you may need to look at your issues around why your friend’s success makes you feel like you bad or less than.

If we look at envy as a shadow trait, then it has nothing to do with the other person. They are just reflecting our desires, our disappointments, and our resentments. Envy usually emerges from unconscious assumptions we formed through attachment issues with our primary caregivers, toxic family systems (e.g., sibling rivalry), and/or an emphasis on overachievement in our families or culture. By going inward and confronting your shadow, you can do the work that will help you move toward your own path and find your unique purpose.

4 Films With Envy-Driven Plots

Here are four award-winning films in which envy drives the story. Each one shows what happens when a character refuses to face their shadow and lets it take over instead.

Amadeus
Source: Orion Pictures

Amadeus (1984): This is probably one of the most memorable and tragic movies because of the Academy Award-winning performance of the envious villain, Antonio Salieri (F. Murray Abraham), the court composer. He goes insane at the thought that Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (Tom Hulce) is a musical genius and that he can never compete or be that one-of-a-kind talent no matter what he does. As a result, he sets out to destroy Mozart's career and pushes him into the Requiem that kills him. Then, Salieri ends up confined to an insane asylum until the end of his life.

The Prestige
Source: Warner Bros. Pictures

The Prestige (2006): In Christopher Nolan’s superb thriller film, two magicians—Robert Angier, aka The Great Danton (Hugh Jackman), and Alfred Borden, aka The Professor (Christian Bale)—are each obsessed with the other’s magical secrets. Angier has money, style, and polish that Borden envies. Borden has the ultimate magic trick, “The Transported Man,” that Angier cannot buy or figure out, and that drives him crazy. Envy (and some revenge) drive them both to want the other to lose no matter what the cost.

All About Eve
Source: 20th Century Fox

All About Eve (1950): In this Best Picture winner, the character Eve (Anne Baxter) does not want to destroy the person she envies; she wants to become her (Bette Davis). Psychologist Elizabeth Li calls this behavior the pursuit of replication of someone else’s life. It is when someone does not just want to learn from you but wants to become you. They want to copy you because they envy what you have (such as success, happiness, or fulfillment). However, someone else’s success and happiness cannot be duplicated. Li calls this one of the “profound misunderstandings of human life.” We can’t just buy a secret formula and replicate someone else’s life; we must do the work on our own lives, with what we have, and build from there.

Parasite
Source: Neon

Parasite (2019): Unlike the other films above, this Academy Award-winning film portrays class envy. The Kim family (Song Kang-ho, Lee Sun-kyun, Cho Yeo-jeong) wants to be like the wealthy Park family. The Kims' scheme is to secure jobs for each family member within the Park household while concealing their true identities. While the Parks are away on a camping trip, the Kims revel in the house's luxuries, but things go horribly wrong after a humiliating incident, and envy turns into violence.

item.title: When and How to Bring Up Sex and Sexuality With Your Child
item.description:
Parenting

When and How to Bring Up Sex and Sexuality With Your Child

It is important to talk to children early and often about their own bodies.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Start talking to your child about their body earlier than you might think.
  • Don't have just one conversation; have many conversations over time.
  • Answer any questions your child has about their body or yours. Stay factual and judgement-free.

Do you bring up sex and sexuality with your kids, or do you wait for them to ask? This question came up in our parenting group yesterday. And opinions were mixed. The mother who asked the question had a 10-year-old who had never asked, and so she had never spoken to her son about sex or sexuality. Another mother told her daughter at age four what sex "is". One mother admitted that she also had never brought up the subject with her 10-year-old. She didn't say she was anxious about doing so but when I mentioned that sometimes the parent is nervous about initiating this conversation, she admitted that this was true for her.

One thing to remember, however, is that your child may also be anxious about talking about their body or about sex. They may feel embarrassed; they may have heard things from their friends, and they may not know what is OK to bring up and what is not.

But children need to know about their bodies, for example, what will happen with their bodies as they reach puberty. They need to know what sex is before they hear about it from a peer, they need to know why people have sex and they need to hear from you about what it means to be ready to have sex with another person. As they get to be young adolescents, they need to know that sex should always be a voluntary act, what "consent" means and that they should always give consent and get consent from the other person when having sexual experiences. And they also need to know all the specifics of birth control and STD prevention.

However, one study showed that by early adolescence, many parents have not discussed birth control efficacy, resisting partner pressure for sex, STD symptoms, condom use, choosing birth control, or partner condom refusal. The same study showed that more than 40% of children have intercourse before any discussion about STD symptoms, condom use, choosing birth control, or partner condom refusal (3).

In a review of this topic, a report from the Guttmacher Institute says that parents can have a significant effect on their children’s sexual risk-taking​ if they talk openly with their children about sex and sexual behavior. But, according to this report, many parents have only limited or no communication on the topic​, often because they feel their children are not ready to hear about it, or because they have negative expectations of the outcomes of talking (3).

One of the things that gets in the way of talking to children about sex and sexuality is that some parents have trouble acknowledging that their children might be​ interested in this subject - - or that by age 12 or 13, they might be sexually active in one way or another​. Many parents​ also lack role models​ for how to talk about sex ​with their children because their own parents did not talk​ to them​ (3).

So, if you do not want to be one of these parents, here is my advice: start talking about your child's body early and don't feel you have to squeeze everything into one or two talks.

Here are the specifics:

  • Starting around two, name bodily parts appropriately for your child.
  • At three, or when they ask, tell them what people of other genders have as body parts.
  • Early on, establish appropriate boundaries: after age two, avoid being naked with your child. Talk about privacy and why you need it when dressing, showering, and going to the bathroom. Starting at around age five, discourage your child from running around naked. Talk about privacy some more. Starting around age six, talk about body boundaries. We don't touch other people's bodies; they should not touch ours.
  • At around four, if your child has not already asked, bring up the conversation about sex by saying, "I want to tell you where babies come from". Keep your explanation simple. If your child has questions, answer them.
  • At around five, begin talking about consent. Your child's pediatrician may have started asking for consent to examine your child's body. If this happens, after the appointment, talk to your child about why the doctor asked for permission and about how any adult touching them should do this. Try not to scare your child, but tell them that no adults other than doctors, nurses, and parents ought to touch their bodies.
  • At every age, when your child asks about your body, answer factually.
  • At around eight, talk to your child about porn. It is a reality that many children have either accidentally or purposefully found porn by this age. Tell them that porn is not helpful for kids to watch, even though they may want to because they are curious. Tell your child that the way bodies look in porn and the things people do are not necessarily the way everyone's body looks or the things everybody wants to do.
  • By 13, begin having more conversations about the importance of treating other people and their bodies and feelings with respect. Talk some more about consent and about pressure. Tell them that you know kids at school are talking about sexual things and even doing sexual things and some ways for them to think about these things.
  • By 13 to 14, be sure to talk about what birth control and STD prevention is and what is available for kids who choose to be sexually active and why it is important to know about these things.
article continues after advertisement

In other words, to cover the topics of sex and sexuality, there have to be many conversations, not just one. And having all of these conversations takes the pressure off parents to make sure they say all the right things during the one big talk.

As the Guttmacher Institute report suggests, if these conversations are hard for you, prepare what you will say ahead of time. Refer to books for help. If your child is taking a sex education class, ask about it and use this as a way to begin the conversation.

And good luck. It's really not as hard as you're afraid it will be!

item.title: Does Better-Looking Mean Better Sex?
item.description:
Body Image

Does Better-Looking Mean Better Sex?

Comparing yourself to others is not good for your sex life.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • How one looks does not determine sexual function or satisfaction.
  • How one feels about how they look influences their sexual experience.
  • Social media use can undermine body image and sexual self-esteem.

Every week, I speak with clients who tell me that their looks interfere with their sex life.

They wish they weighed less, had more hair on their head and less everywhere else, or had a bigger this or smaller that. During sex, some of them keep their T-shirts on and the lights off.

The literature says that people's objective beauty has little connection to how much they enjoy sex. Lots of nice-looking people don't enjoy sex, and lots of plain-looking people do.

What does apparently matter is how people feel about their bodies. Regardless of what they actually look like, people who feel attractive want sex more, have sex more, and typically enjoy it more. Studies show that this is true for both men and women. (1)

On the other hand, people who judge their bodies harshly (regardless of what they actually look like) are less likely to desire sex, and less likely to believe that they are sexually desired.

Although unfortunate, this is understandable: Sexual enjoyment depends on being present. Concerns about your looks are the opposite of being present: It involves self-consciousness, worrying about a partner's (lack of) enjoyment, and judging yourself.

So it's true that if you feel unattractive, it's harder to enjoy sex. But in a world of media images and looksmaxxing; popular enhancements to skin, teeth, and hair; steroids, peptides, testosterone, and GLP-1s; fitspiration videos and cosmetic surgery, who feels attractive enough?

Now, Add Social Media

And then, there's social media. Interestingly, it's not simply the raw number of minutes watched each day that drives body dissatisfaction (and therefore reduced sexual enjoyment). A crucial part of what undermines users' sex lives is how much they compare their appearance to others.

When people compare themselves to movie stars, they're looking at another species of human being. But on social media, people are invited to compare themselves to non-celebrities—allegedly ordinary people you could supposedly look like if only you tried harder. That's what makes social media so deadly for many people's body image, and therefore their sex life.

Here's an interesting experimental finding: After viewing social media profiles of attractive age-peers, participants felt worse about their own bodies than participants who viewed less-attractive profiles. (2)

In fact, repeated exposure to being evaluated on appearance causes people to internalize an outside observer's viewpoint of their own body. Social media users who do a lot of comparing unconsciously learn to judge themselves the way they imagine others judge them. They develop a habit of monitoring their own appearance until, as uncomfortable as it is, it seems normal.

Predictably, people who engage more frequently with social media report competitive pressure to curate an attractive online persona, encouraging others to do their own self-harming comparisons.

So the problem isn't just "social media" in the abstract; it's the self-surveillance and comparison habits it cultivates.

Thus, if you want to enjoy sex more, you need to decide that you're attractive enough, whatever that means to you. Even better, decide that how you look is irrelevant to your eligibility for sexual satisfaction. It would also help to view less social media, and when you do, make a conscious decision that you won't compare yourself to your (supposed) peers.

Because your sexual satisfaction is at stake—which isn't trivial, is it?

item.title: How Radical Acceptance Can Help Children of Gray Divorce
item.description:
Divorce

How Radical Acceptance Can Help Children of Gray Divorce

Often, children are still trying to heal years after the parents' gray divorce.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • High-conflict gray divorce can leave adult children stuck in grief years later.
  • Accepting painful facts, without resistance, can help end needless suffering.
  • Radical acceptance means facing reality, not approving of what happened.

This is the first post in this series.

My therapy dog, Friede, and I met Olivia, 25, in the waiting area. She invited Friede to join her on the sofa and began.

"I'm so glad you have Friede. The therapy dog at my rehab facility helped me so much in my recovery. Every day, his understanding eyes locked onto mine, and his unconditional love washed over me. Oh, and it's nice to meet you, too, Dr. Hughes!" She smiled and rolled her eyes in feigned embarrassment.

A therapy dog in a session with a patient.
Source: jacob-mcgowin/Unsplash

"It's OK," I said. "I'm accustomed to playing second fiddle to Friede."

Olivia settled on the love seat in my office. "My aftercare program referred me to you. I also have a sponsor in Alcoholics Anonymous. I'll be brief." She continued in a hurried, staccato style, like she was marching in lockstep.

"I know I wrote most of this in the questionnaires for you, but I want you to hear my words out loud. Is that OK?"

"Yes, of course."

"I'm an only child. Besides Mom and Dad, my aunts, uncles, cousins, and grandparents were my family. My parents divorced at 50 when I was 10. My life changed overnight. It was a high-conflict divorce that lasted for over eight years. I had a minor's counsel, a good man, who helped me as much as he could. Some of our relatives lined up on Dad's side, some on Mom's side. I lived amid constant bad-mouthing from all sides. I felt like I was living in a war zone, which I was." Her eyes filled with tears and her right foot tapped nervously on the floor. Closing her eyes, she inhaled a long, deep breath.

Speaking slowly and calmly, I encouraged her. "Revisiting all of it is difficult. Take as long as you need."

She inhaled another slow, deep breath. "The portrait of my large family with smiling faces that always hung above the fireplace vanished. What remained was the blank space. I lived in that emptiness. I was bonded with my family members. They were my identity. I struggled through high school, college, and grad school, trying to figure out who I was. I've done a lot of therapy. I started drinking in college. I went to treatment to get sober. I have a little over three years of sobriety. Overall, my life is good. I like my job and have a good, supportive friend group, but I still feel stuck."

article continues after advertisement

"How are you stuck?" I asked.

"It keeps replaying in my mind. I hear, 'How could my parents have been so ignorant about how their fighting and hatred was affecting me? How could my family not see me, that little girl, who was hurting so much, losing so much of her life, and feeling so empty? They all went on obliviously with their lives! The adults and their kids on both sides of my family just walked away like the Red Sea that parted in the Bible story. I felt so alone!"

She sobbed. I recalled the Pulitzer Prize-winning novelist Toni Morrison’s depiction of grief: “It was a fine cry—loud and long—but it had no bottom and it had no top, just circles and circles of sorrow.” I handed her a copy of the quote.

"This is one of my favorite quotes about grief. How does it land on you?"

"It's exactly how I've felt over and over. Have I been grieving all these years?"

"Yes. As Morrison says, grieving isn't a linear process. Your loss and pain are profound, Olivia. I'm so sorry it's been so long."

After several minutes of silence, she pulled Friede closer to her, raised her head, looked at me, and proclaimed in a determined voice, "It feels good to dump all of that! Thank you. I'm ready to move on."

"I want to acknowledge what a strong woman you are. As you shared with me, the image of the mythical phoenix bird came to mind. You have pursued a lot of healing and risen from the ashes of your family of origin. Yet you feel stuck and still suffer. You know AA's Serenity Prayer: accepting what we cannot change, having the courage to change what we can, and the wisdom to know the difference. What meaning have you taken from it?"

article continues after advertisement

Her eyes fell to Friede, still snuggled beside her. Her previously determined voice faded into barely audible words. "I've never liked that prayer. It makes me sad."

"How so?"

"The 'accept the things I cannot change' part."

"Hmm. What meaning do you make of that?"

Gently stroking Friede's head and back for several minutes, she whispered as though wishing her words weren't true. "That I'm stuck because I'm struggling with acceptance." Her voice fell at the end of the sentence in a tone that indicated accuracy. She raised her gaze to mine. "Now what?"

"I love word origins. Our word 'accept' derives from the Latin word meaning 'take to oneself, to receive.' Not 'to agree or approve.' Think of it as being present with something that exists. Fifteen years ago, you couldn't 'receive' your parents' divorce and the losses that followed. It was forced on you. Today, as the woman you are, you can open your hands and 'receive' the fact that it all happened, rather than resist it with closed fists. What would open hands feel like?"

She moved her right arm off Friede, joining it with her left hand on her lap. She slowly turned her palms upward. Friede moved her head from Olivia's side and rested it between her hands. We sat quietly, present in the moment.

Several minutes passed. "Olivia, you may know that our bodies and our words speak. What are you noticing?"

"Maybe I'm feeling the serenity in the prayer that I've never felt before. I'm willing to keep my hands open."

"I think you're right. Here comes another of my digressions! The Serenity Prayer holds age-old and present-day wisdom. Philosopher Epictetus, born into slavery in the Roman Empire, said, 'Some things are in our control, and others not.' Dr. Marsha Linehan, who experienced mental illness and suicidality as a young woman, developed the therapeutic skill of radical acceptance in the 1980s from Zen Buddhist teaching and said, 'Pain is pain. Suffering, agony, are pain plus non-acceptance.'"

"Would you be willing to do an assignment for our next session?"

"Yes. I want to end my suffering."

"OK. Here's a handout about radical acceptance with exercises to complete that can help you move past the suffering."

Patient name and details changed to preserve confidentiality.

item.title: Anxiety: Its Meaning and Management
item.description:
Anxiety

Anxiety: Its Meaning and Management

What is anxiety and how can we manage it more constructively?

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety is an inescapable and existential part of the human condition.
  • Avoiding or repressing existential anxiety can lead to pathological anxiety.
  • Anxiety is related to worry and stress.

This is Part 1 of a series of posts on anxiety.

Anxiety.
Source: Jayberries/Wikimedia Commons

Anxiety, sometimes called the “great imitator” because of its ability to mimic and assume various forms of physical and psychological symptoms, can manifest in myriad ways, one of which is persistent, excessive worrying. According to the American Psychiatric Association, in generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), excessive anxiety and worry (apprehensive expectation) about events such as school or work performance have been present more days than not for a period of at least six months. By definition, this incessant worrying is difficult to control and causes clinically significant distress and/or impairment in social, occupational or other daily activities.

Ironically, worrying—which is often an attempt to anticipate and prevent bad things from happening—tends to make us even more anxious, creating a never-ending and constantly escalating cycle of anxiety: worry, stress, more anxiety, more worry, etc. Why do we worry as much as we do? What exactly is it we worry about? And how might we learn to worry a little less?

First and foremost, we worry because we fear the future. The unknown. We worry about what will happen to us, our family, our partner, our business, our income, our savings, our home, our possessions, our country, our world, the cosmos, etc. Will there be nuclear war? Cataclysmic natural disaster? Serious illness? Loss? Divorce? Legal problems? Economic meltdown? Terrorist attacks? Mass shootings? Political assassinations? We live in a universe that is inherently unpredictable, dangerous, and deadly. Indeed, anxiety can be understood existentially as an acute, subliminal, or subconscious awareness of life's intrinsic insecurity—and, ultimately, the ever-present possibility and absolute inescapability of death. So much of what we worry about has to do with losing what we have: health, happiness, love, wealth, power, status, freedom, independence, support, and, finally, life itself either through making some tragic mistake or due to the inevitable vagaries of fate.

Existential vs. Pathological Anxiety

Anxiety is a ubiquitous phenomenon in our day. But not all anxiety is neurotic or pathological. In his book The Meaning of Anxiety (1950/1977), existential psychoanalyst Rollo May makes a crucial distinction between normal anxiety and pathological anxiety, suggesting that neurotic or even psychotic anxiety typically stems from the chronic avoidance of normal or existential anxiety. In other words, when we refuse to accept and tolerate anxiety as an inevitable element of human existence (anxiety is the "dizziness" of our experience of existential freedom, says Soren Kierkegaard), we paradoxically set ourselves up for the appearance of pathological anxiety and neurotic (or, in some cases, psychotic) worrying. The painful and debilitating symptoms of panic disorder or obsessive-compulsive disorder, and, in the extreme, persecutory delusions, are prime examples of pathological anxiety.

article continues after advertisement

Existential or normal anxiety, on the other hand, derives from a recognition, either conscious or unconscious, that existence is finite, tenuous, dangerous, and unpredictable, and that all or what little we possess can be taken from us at any time. This is why, for example, we worry so much about making important choices or decisions: We don't want to decide without knowing with certainty the outcome, which, of course, can never be guaranteed. So we procrastinate (see my prior post), trying to evade the existential anxiety, freedom, and responsibility of choosing. (As philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre said, even not choosing is still a choice.) Instead of deciding, we succumb to our anxiety and worry instead or decide and then obsessively worry that it was the wrong decision.

Anxiety and Fear of Exposure

Anxious worrying can also pertain to wanting to be perceived by the world as we wish, and desiring to see ourselves as we want to be seen. When we are heavily invested in projecting and maintaining a certain image or persona to others, we must be ever vigilant and guarded about that mask being penetrated and seen through. We worry about being exposed. Seen. Found out, judged, and criticized, as, for example, in the so-called "imposter syndrome." And we worry about having to face ourselves. About being confronted with who and what we truly are. We humans harbor a primal fear of the unconscious, the unknown, and of what C.G. Jung (1961) termed the shadow. The persona, as Jung (1961) pointed out, is specifically designed to conceal our shadow, to keep us from fully knowing ourselves as well as to deceive others. For many, the convincing persona of a competent, confident adult disguises an anxious, insecure, worried little girl or boy trying to survive in a terrifying grown-up world.

Social phobia (social anxiety disorder) is an example of such neurotic anxiety. Any circumstance that potentiates embarrassing exposure, suddenly revealing the real person behind the facade, is felt to be profoundly threatening. Anticipatory anxiety kicks in: What if I can't hide my feelings? My insecurity? My shame? My love? My hatred? My sadness? My anger? My neediness? My vulnerability? My true self? Paradoxically, what many try so hard to hide and worry so much about others seeing is the fact that they feel anxiety in the first place. We worry about what people will think of us if they discover we suffer from anxieties, inferiority feelings, or insecurities, forgetting that every human has such feelings. So, we work extra hard and worry constantly about how to hide our anxiety, which only makes it stronger and doubly difficult to disguise.

Stress and Anxiety

Anxiety is closely correlated with "stress." Often, when people speak of being “stressed,” they are referring to feeling overwhelmed and anxious. Some anxious worrying and concern for the future may be unavoidable, and, in certain situations, even necessary and potentially helpful. We need the capacity for anxiety to anticipate danger, detect and deal with fundamental threats to our basic survival, consider possible outcomes, motivate and energize us, warn us when we have betrayed our values, and to become more fully conscious and creative. But when we try to avoid or escape anxiety by denying reality and our true feelings, it turns toxic, taking the pathological form of excessive worrying, chronic fatigue, insomnia, tension headaches, hypervigilance, irritability, agitation, impaired concentration, digestive problems, and other debilitating physical and psychological symptoms. Our ceaseless worrying and self-induced stress has now made us sick. And then we worry about having these symptoms, engendering even greater anxiety and stress. This can become a vicious cycle.

article continues after advertisement

Since stress can cause anxiety and anxiety can cause stress, the first line of treatment, after a physiological source of the anxiety has been medically ruled out, is usually some form of “stress management.” Basic stress management consists of three key components: getting sufficient quantity and quality of sleep, eating properly, and, perhaps most importantly, engaging in regular (preferably daily) physical activity, like cardiovascular exercise on a treadmill, swimming, running, lifting weights, climbing stairs, bicycling, or taking long walks. For most patients who are physically able to engage in strenuous activity, doing so on a regular basis can be helpful in lowering (though not eliminating) their anxiety level. Practicing meditation regularly can also be effective. But, for some, this self-help approach is not enough to sufficiently mitigate their stress and anxiety. In such cases, psychotherapy and/or psychopharmacology may be needed.

item.title: 10 Liabilities of AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

10 Liabilities of AI

Why the politicization of AI is not a small problem.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • The AI revolution is being politicized.
  • The problems that are emerging regarding the AI revolution cut across so many spheres of life for all of us.
  • Allowing for the politicization of AI could lead to a catastrophic future.
Source: Vladimir Shipitsin/Pexels

I was stunned by a recent New York Post cover page. The headline was this: Far-Left Group that Silicon Valley Wants to Lead our Tech-Led Future: The Woke Wizards of A.I.

The messaging of that headline is, to my mind, cause for major concern, because it politicizes issues of AI development.

So many issues seem to get politicized (put into either the politically left bucket or the politically right bucket), regardless of whether they inherently relate to political ideology (Motyl, 2018). Our minds lean toward putting information into neat categories (Billig & Tajfel, 1973). The internet amplifies this effect (Motyl, 2018). This all helps to explain why people often associate pickup trucks and cowboy hats with the political right and granola and paper straws with the political left. Our minds naturally tend to categorize things this way.

As I see it, AI is not a partisan issue. It is a human issue.

10 Reasons to Be Concerned About AI

Below are 10 reasons that all humans should be concerned about where the AI boom is taking us.

1. AI is making us dumber.

In the age of AI, cognitive skills are reducing (see Gerlich, 2025). How could it not? AI does the thinking for us. And when we stop exercising our mental muscles, we lose cognitive sharpness (see Cherrier et al., 2021). Not that complicated.

2. AI content can be racist and sexist.

LLM versions of AI have been "trained" on existing content across the documented human experience—a history replete with sexism and racism. Consider the fact that the top AI image related to "evolution" recently showed as a progression of non-human primates morphing into a black man morphing into a white man with blond hair. Very offensive. Check out this post of mine that focuses on this issue.

3. AI can cultivate fraud.

Using AI, students are submitting "papers" by simply typing a prompt into AI. People are doctoring their photos with unparalleled technology. Some professors are submitting academic work that has been nearly 100% created by AI. And more. People are lying to each other and misrepresenting themselves in various ways with the help of AI.

4. AI is wreaking havoc on intimate relationships.

People across the industrialized world are having consensual sex with other humans less than ever (see Twenge, 2020). Many are turning to AI for relationship gratification. For a deep-dive into the effects of AI on intimacy, I recommend that you check out Marianne Brandon's blog, The Future of Intimacy. More than a little eye-opening.

5. AI is starting to replace therapists.

People are often turning to AI for therapy and counseling. Sometimes this takes the form of people simply leaning on AI for answers to issues in their lives. Sometimes it takes the form of actually having an AI therapist. In multiple cases, AI used in this way has led to disaster, including this teen suicide that was reportedly shaped by "guidance" provided by AI—including an offer to write this young person's suicide note.

6. AI produces slop.

The products of generative AI are very often of low quality. "Writing" samples that are AI-generated often say nothing at all. And AI often gets facts wrong. I recently ran into a case in which an author submitted a draft of a chapter that included multiple references to work that doesn't exist. So many people today are in the unenviable position of having to figure out what is AI-generated as opposed to human-generated. And so many are cleaning up AI slop for hours as part of our work. As is addressed in this article in the Guardian, this is soul-sucking work.

7. AI breaches data security.

Recently, AI "agents" infiltrated a major health database in Australia, accessing supposedly private information. If that is happening in 2026, just think about what it is going to be capable of in 2036. If you are not worried about AI technologies stealing your identity, gutting your bank account, etc., then you are not paying attention.

8. AI is built on stolen property.

Modern AI models are largely based on stolen property. I am one of thousands and thousands of authors who is part of a 10-figure settlement against Anthropic—the parent company of Claude. In creating Claude, Anthropic literally used tons of copyrighted material (mostly in the form of published books) to "train" AI. This is disgusting.

9. AI is gutting our capacity to write.

Among the many cognitive skills that are being adversely affected by AI, writing is right up there. We now live in a world in which students who are supposed to be taught writing skills can take the easy way out and produce "papers" that are largely or completely written by AI. How will they learn how to write? Implications are staggering (see Al-Adawi, 2025).

10. Think about the kids.

Advances in computer technologies have wreaked havoc on the emotional and cognitive lives of kids in recent years. Cellphone technology and social media have been implicated in cyberbullying, which is highly prevalent across the world, along with mental health issues among teens (Twenge et al., 2019). The AI boom is amplifying all of it. For a deep-dive into the adverse effects of technology on the next generation, check out this post by Jean Twenge.

Bottom Line

This post is designed as a research-based word of caution regarding the politicization of the AI boom. Given our evolved psychological tendencies to quickly categorize all kinds of issues in "us versus them" terms (Tajfel & Billig, 1973), people regularly put all kinds of things into political categories. These days, the American flag and NASCAR seem to be treasures of the political right, while NPR and recycling initiatives seem to be treasures of the political left. In his research on the nature of political polarization, Matt Motyl (2018) makes a strong case that such political polarization is steeped in our nature.

Given that so many issues end up landing into cultural buckets that represent conservative versus progressive political orientations, any novel social issue has strong potential to be politicized. Unfortunately, it looks like attitudes about the future of AI in our world are starting to morph into political attitudes.

I hope that this development gives anyone pause. The number of problems for humans that are emerging on the heels of the AI boom is staggering. The list of 10 such issues presented here is simply the tip of one of the largest icebergs in human history.

The AI issue is not an issue of the political left or right. It is a human issue. And losing the battle to the robots is not an option.

item.title: The Social Power of the Pause
item.description:
First Impressions

The Social Power of the Pause

How taking a breath facilitates cooperation and chemistry.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Pausing is helpful in collaborative conversation, as long as they don't go on too long.
  • Pauses longer than three seconds are awkward, unpleasant, and occasionally even suspicious.
  • Short pauses encourage assents, which are affirmative statements of understanding such as "uh-huh."

First impressions are enduring, and often engaging. Most people come away from an initial conversation with an impression based not so much on the other person’s appearance, experience, or resume, but how the other person made them feel. Because initial conversations can determine whether conversation partners will talk again, potential partners want to approach a first meeting in a fashion that is likely to spark a second. That means, according to research, take time to share, then time to pause.

Source: Rachel Scott/Pixabay

The Power of the Pause to Prompt Positivity

Alex B. Van Zant et al. (2025) studied the impact of pausing in collaborative conversations—defined as “cooperative, task-oriented dialogues” where two or more people collaborate in pursuit of a common goal.[i] They studied collaborative conversations, including an examination of customer service calls, and two experiments manipulating the frequency of pauses. They found that long silences can negatively impact impression management, but in a collaborative context, brief pauses while speaking can enhance perception of a person’s helpfulness because they encourage assent from conversation partners.

These findings have implications both personally and professionally.

Chemistry, Charisma, and Collaboration

Van Zant et al. recognize that although collaborators have the same goal, they do not always share their partners’ understanding of the situation at hand, or their ideas about how to approach it. This requires collaboration partners to attempt to understand each other’s positions in order to accommodate and incorporate their views. Consequently, the collaboration process begins with establishing common ground, including shared beliefs, assumptions, and facts.

Allowing conversation partners to inject understanding while speakers talk permits conversation partners the chance to provide positive feedback without taking over the conversation, prompting collaboration in furtherance of achieving a shared mutual understanding. To this end, pauses can be helpful; as long as they are not too long.

In Productive Conversation, Silence Is Not Golden

Regarding the length of conversational silence, Van Zant et al. note that it takes about 0.3 seconds for conversation partners to perceive and react to a pause, and such periods of silence may indicate a speaker is thinking. When silence continues for too long, on the other hand, it can express a speaker’s discomfort or difficulty articulating coherent thoughts. How long is too long? Van Zant et al. note it takes an average of three seconds for silences to become uncomfortable, prompting conversation partners to feel compelled to retake the speaking floor, or change the subject. Silences of three seconds or longer are thus perceived as awkward or disruptive to a natural conversation.

But it gets worse. Van Zant et al. note that long silences may signal a speaker’s discomfort with a conversation topic, or cause conversation partners to worry they said something inappropriate or suggested something the speaker is struggling to find a way to express polite disagreement. In addition, they note that long silences can indicate that a speaker is having a hard time articulating a coherent thought, or perhaps even worse, is “buying time” to create a lie.

Agreeableness as Attractive Through Assent

While long pauses create awkwardness, Van Zant et al. explain that short pauses encourage assent. Assents are “affirmative signals of understanding” such as “OK” and “uh-huh,” indicating listening, understanding, or agreement. These responses prompt mutual understanding through providing positive feedback to speakers that a conversation partner accepts or understands what is being conveyed.

I would add to this finding that the art of bonding through strategic conversational pausing is effective when collaborating with colleagues as well as courting romantic interests. Bonding through common ground is a solid foundation upon which to build a relationship, and pausing briefly when speaking demonstrates authentic interest in the other person, attention when they are speaking, and respect for their opinions and viewpoints. And that is an attractive way to spark chemistry when starting a new relationship.

Living Life on Autopilot? 3 Steps to Find Your Vitality

What childhood emotional neglect does to your vitality, and how to get it back.

Posted September 28, 2026

Key points
  • Feeling bored, numb, or vaguely alone can be a sign that you are living on autopilot.
  • Autopilot means you do not have enough access to your own emotions to feel your own life.
  • Your emotions are still there, and getting back in touch with them is a learnable skill.
Source: Nina Lawrenson/peopleimages.com

Do you feel bored in your life?

Do you enjoy happy occasions less than you should?

Do you sometimes feel emotionally numb?

Do other people seem to experience more intense joy, love, or closeness than you do?

Do you sometimes question the purpose and value of your life?

Do you put others' needs before your own?

If you answered "yes" to two or more of the questions above, it may be a sign that you're on autopilot. What does this mean? It means that you do not have enough access to your true emotions.

In my work as a psychologist, I have heard many people express these concerns. Almost all have been fine, good-hearted people who are successful in many areas of their lives. But for them, something is missing. Some mysterious ingredient that makes life feel full, rich, and stimulating is simply lacking for them.

I worked for over a decade to determine what had happened to these good people to cause them to feel this way. What I discovered was surprising. The answer lay not in anything that had happened to them. It lay instead in what had failed to happen for them.

Where the Sense of Autopilot Comes From

Almost without exception, these folks' parents failed to provide them with emotional validation in childhood. They had grown up in families in which emotion was not noticed, responded to, or valued enough. In other words, they had grown up with some amount of childhood emotional neglect.

Through their parents' lack of responsiveness, each of these folks had received an indirect, subtle message. The message was "Your feelings don't matter." When a child receives this message, they cope with it automatically. Without realizing it, they push their feelings down and away, so they won't bother anyone.

As an adult, they will have no memory that their emotional needs were not met in childhood, and no awareness that they pushed their feelings away. Instead, gradually over time, they will become accustomed to living without them. They will march through their life with a smile on their face, providing for the needs of others, but out of tune with themselves.

They will know how to provide care, but not how to receive it. They will know how to help others, but not how to accept help themselves. And underneath it all, even when surrounded by people who love them, they will sometimes feel deeply, curiously, alone.

And please know, this is so often no one's fault. Many emotionally neglectful parents are doing their best, and most were raised in the very same way themselves.

Why You Need to Tap Into Vitality

Most people don't realize how vital their emotions are to their own health and happiness. Emotions are our body's way of talking to us. Anger tells us to protect ourselves. Passion drives us to create. Hurt tells us to take care.

And through it all, by feeling our feelings, we experience the fullness and richness of life. Emotion informs us and connects us. It enlivens and enriches, and gives us meaning and purpose. Emotion is the spice of life.

So what does a person do who is feeling bored, empty, numb, or alone? What if you suspect that your emotions are pushed away and that you are living your life on autopilot?

The good news is that you can take over the wheel. Your emotions are still there, and you can get back in touch with them. Here are some basic steps to start this process.

Three Steps to Recovering Emotional Vitality

  1. Own and accept the problem. This first step is actually the biggest. I have found that when a person recognizes that they are rejecting this vital part of themselves – their emotions – a whole new world opens up for them. Accept the problem, that it's not your fault, and that you can fix it.
  2. Increase your emotional awareness. Make a decision to start tuning in to what you are feeling. Identifying and naming what you feel is a learnable skill. In a few minutes a day, you can change your life.
  3. Work hard to put your own needs first. Taking care of yourself must happen before you can take care of others. It is hard to give other people something you don't have yourself.

Back in the Driver's Seat

Whether you need protection, care, strength, connection, warmth, joy, meaning, or purpose, listen to your body's messages. Tune in. Pay attention.

Because, believe it or not, your emotions will take you off autopilot and put you into the driver's seat, where you are in control. Where you are fully living. And where you belong.
